sentences: A few years ago, climbing was a rare sport, reserved for the mountains.
Today, you can find climbing gyms in almost every major city.
In these gyms, people climb on artificial walls, with holds of all colors.
Each color indicates a route, more or less difficult.
You can therefore start slowly and progress at your own pace.
Many people think that climbing mainly requires strength.
In reality, it is also a sport of strategy.
Before climbing, you need to observe the wall and choose where to place your hands and feet.
Climbing is often done in pairs.
One person climbs, while the other holds the rope and ensures their safety.
So, you need to trust your partner.

sentences: Abroad, you can find French restaurants in almost every major city.
However, what is served there doesn't always resemble what a French person would eat at home.
The dishes are often adapted to local tastes.
A recipe can become sweeter, spicier, or heartier, depending on the country.
Some purists are outraged: for them, it's almost a betrayal.
However, one can see things differently.
A cuisine that travels is a living cuisine.
As it moves from one country to another, a dish transforms, mixes with other traditions, and sometimes gives birth to something new.
After all, French cuisine itself has developed over the centuries by borrowing products and ideas from elsewhere.
Therefore, it is not necessary for a dish to remain identical for it to have value.
What matters is perhaps less the fidelity to a recipe than the pleasure one experiences at the table.

sentences: Between twenty-five and thirty-five, my physical activity was limited to running after the bus.
Work, fatigue, and evening series: I always had a great excuse.
I kept telling myself, 'I'll get back to it next month' — and those next months piled up for ten years.
The trigger came from a mundane scene.
While climbing four flights of stairs with my groceries, on the day the elevator was out of order, I arrived out of breath as if I had just run a marathon.
At thirty-five, four flights of stairs brought me to my knees.
That evening, I decided to get back to it.
For real.
My first attempt was an instructive disaster.
Full of enthusiasm, I put on my old sneakers and went out to run 'like before.'
I lasted twelve minutes.
The next three days, I discovered muscles I didn't even know existed, simply because they hurt.
My motivation died along with my soreness, and the sneakers went back into the closet for two months.
It was a doctor friend who explained my mistake: 'You want to make up for ten years in a week.
Your heart is ready to progress quickly, but your tendons and joints need months.
Start ridiculously small.
' Ridiculously small.
Those words changed everything.
Second attempt, new method: twenty minutes of brisk walking, twice a week.
It was almost too easy — and that was exactly the goal.
It's impossible to find an excuse against twenty minutes.
After a month, I moved to three sessions alternating walking and slow running.
Then running gradually replaced walking.
A year later, the results exceeded everything I hoped for.
I run for forty-five minutes without suffering, three times a week.
I sleep deeply, whereas I used to wake up every night.
My back, which had troubled me for years at the office, has calmed down.
And the four flights?
I climb them while talking on the phone.
If you find yourself in the same situation I was in, here’s what I wish I had heard earlier.
Start smaller than your pride would like.
Aim for consistency, not performance: two sessions completed are better than five sessions dreamed of.
Expect a dip in motivation around the third week — it passes.
And find pleasure in the activity itself, otherwise you won't last.
The body surprisingly forgives years of neglect.
It only asks that you return to it with patience.

sentences: The first time I came across a group of Nordic walkers in my park, I admit, I smiled.
About ten people were walking energetically with ski poles — in the middle of June, with not a snowflake in sight.
It looked like a joke, or a strange trend from elsewhere.
I was wrong to smile, and this article is my way of acknowledging that.
Where does this practice come from?
From Finland, as its name suggests.
In the 1930s, Finnish cross-country skiers were looking for a way to train in the summer, without snow.
They kept the poles and left the skis.
The method was refined, specific poles were created, and Nordic walking became a sport in its own right, now practiced by millions of people in Europe.
But why on earth walk with poles?
That's the whole difference from ordinary walking.
When we walk normally, our arms swing for nothing: all the work comes from the legs.
With the poles, each step is accompanied by a push from the arms.
As a result: the shoulders, arms, chest, and back join in.
Experts estimate that Nordic walking engages about eighty percent of the body's muscles, compared to barely half for regular walking.
You burn significantly more energy — without realizing it, because the effort is distributed across the whole body.
The other big advantage is the gentleness.
Unlike running, there is no impact with each step: the joints — knees, hips, ankles — are spared, and the poles even relieve some of the body weight.
That's why this sport is suitable for almost everyone: recovering athletes, elderly people, complete beginners, overweight individuals.
Everyone moves at their own pace, and the group adapts.
Last month, pushed by my neighbor — seventy years old and with calves of steel — I finally tried it.
Immediate lesson in humility: the technique doesn't come naturally.
For twenty minutes, my arms and legs refused to coordinate, under the amused gaze of the group.
Then the movement came, natural, fluid, almost hypnotic.
An hour later, I was warm all over, my mind clear, and I had signed up for the following Saturday.
Moral: beware of sports that make you smile.
They are often the ones that last.
And if you come across a group of pole walkers in your park, don't smile too quickly.
In a month, it might be you.

sentences: There is a cruel irony at the heart of modern tourism.
What drives millions of people to travel — the desire to discover unique, preserved places filled with beauty and history — is precisely what, as it multiplies, destroys these places.
We love Venice, so we go there; and because twenty million of us love it every year, we gradually suffocate the city we came to admire.
Mass tourism is this contradiction that has become the landscape.
That travel is a beautiful thing, no sensible person would dispute.
Moving around, meeting other ways of living, stepping out of the narrowness of one's own world: nothing has done more for the opening of minds.
The problem is therefore not traveling.
It relates to a purely quantitative phenomenon, whose effects change in nature on a large scale.
One visitor enriches a place; a million visitors, concentrated in the same alleys at the same seasons, crush it.
It's not a question of individual morality — each of these travelers is perfectly legitimate — but of accumulation.
The consequences, in the most affected cities, are now visible to all.
Residents are being driven out by rising rents, as housing is transformed into short-term rentals.
Everyday businesses — the baker, the shoemaker, the grocer — are giving way to identical souvenir shops from one city to another.
The city emptied of its inhabitants becomes a backdrop, a giant postcard that one crosses without ever living there again.
The place survives; its soul departs.
In the face of this, tentative responses are emerging.
Some cities limit the number of visitors, implement reservations, charge entry fees, or ban the largest ships.
These measures, often criticized, at least have the merit of acknowledging the problem and refusing fatalism.
However, they face a formidable difficulty: tourism supports entire regions, and one cannot close the floodgates without depriving of income those whom one claims to protect.
The balance is delicate.
But the actions of cities do not exempt us from more personal reflection.
Each of us, as travelers, has some leeway.
Is it really necessary to go to the same place as everyone else, at the same time?
Should we reduce a region to its three most photographed sites, which we 'do' in a day before leaving?

Traveling off-season, stepping away from the crowds, staying longer in one place, showing interest in less famous spots that are just waiting to be loved: these are all ways to continue discovering the world without contributing to its degradation.
Mass tourism places us in front of an uncomfortable but salutary question.
To love a place, is it to rush there with the crowd?
Or is it, sometimes, to know how to visit it differently — even to renounce it, so that it remains what we came to seek?

sentences: There is a fact that is often cited without realizing its strangeness: no known human culture, at any time, has lived without music.
All societies sing, create rhythms, make instruments, and dance.
However, music, unlike language or tool-making, provides no obvious advantage for survival: you don't feed on a melody, and you don't defend yourself with a rhythm.
So why is this apparently useless activity so universal, and why does it exert a power over us that no other form of art can match?
This question intrigues scientists, and the answers they are beginning to outline are fascinating.
Brain imaging has first revealed a remarkable thing: there is no 'music center' in the brain.
Listening to a piece, on the contrary, activates a vast and distributed network — the areas of sound, of course, but also those of memory, movement, and especially emotions and reward.
This explains phenomena that everyone knows from experience.
Why does a song irresistibly make us want to move?
Because music activates the motor circuits, as if the body is preparing to dance even before we decide to.
Why does a melody bring back, intact, a memory from twenty years ago?
Because it is deeply linked to memory — to the point that it reaches patients who have almost forgotten everything, in whom a song from their youth suddenly revives their gaze and words.
The most mysterious aspect remains the link with emotion.
How can simple vibrations of air, organized according to certain rules, move us to tears?
One clue lies in the notion of expectation.

Our brain, without our knowing it, constantly anticipates the progression of music; and pleasure arises from the subtle interplay between what it predicts and what occurs — an expected resolution that soothes, a surprise that captivates.
The skilled composer plays on our expectations like an instrument.
Music moves us because it secretly dialogues with our mind's incessant predictions.
These discoveries have concrete implications, beyond mere curiosity.
Today, music is used in medicine — to alleviate pain, assist rehabilitation after a brain injury, and reach patients whom words can no longer reach.
Moreover, learning to play an instrument in childhood seems to leave lasting traces: studies suggest benefits for concentration, memory, and even certain language abilities.
Music is not just a pleasure; it shapes the brain that practices it.
Should we, then, explain everything?
Many mysteries still resist, and it is not certain that science will ever fully elucidate why a sequence of sounds can move us.
But there is a beautiful lesson here: understanding the mechanisms does not abolish emotion.
Knowing how a rainbow works does not diminish its beauty; knowing the circuits of music does not take away the thrill it provides.
We do not need to understand music for it to touch us.
But discovering how deeply it is embedded in our brain adds yet another reason to marvel at this old companion of humanity.

sentences: Buy now, pay later.
This promise is everywhere: in stores, online, at the end of our online purchases.
Consumer credit has made almost everything immediately accessible, without having to wait to save up.
It's convenient, sometimes useful, but it's also a trap that many people fall into.
The principle of credit is simple: a bank or a store lends you money for a purchase, and you pay it back little by little, each month.
The problem is that this money isn't free.
In exchange for the loan, you have to pay interest.
In other words, the item bought on credit ends up costing more — sometimes much more — than its displayed price.
The danger comes from the ease of it.
Since you don't pay right away, you feel like the expense is small: "only thirty euros a month."
But these small monthly payments add up.
You take out a loan for a sofa, another for a phone, another for a vacation, and soon a large part of your salary goes each month to repayments.
That's how you end up in debt without even realizing it.
Credit isn't bad in itself.
Borrowing can make sense for an important and lasting project, like housing, or in case of a real necessity.
But you should always ask yourself the same question before signing: am I borrowing for a real need, or just because I don't have the patience to save?
The wisest rule can be summed up in one sentence: never go into debt for a fleeting pleasure.
The sofa will be old long before the debt is paid off, and you'll continue to pay for an item you no longer enjoy.
In the face of advertising that pushes you to consume right away, the old habit of waiting and saving is often the most rewarding — and the most peaceful.

sentences: Last Sunday, there was a flea market in my neighborhood.
The whole main street was closed to cars.
The residents were selling their old items in front of their houses.
I love flea markets: you never know what you will find.
I arrived early, around nine o'clock.
You could find everything: clothes, books, toys, bikes, records.
First, I looked at the books.
A man was selling his entire library.
And then, surprise: I found a book from my childhood, the same one I read when I was ten.
I bought it for one euro.
Further along, a lady was selling an old radio.
"Does it still work?" I asked.
She plugged it in, and the radio lit up with a nice old sound.
I hesitated, but it was a bit too expensive for me.
At the flea market, you have to negotiate.
It's part of the game!
A seller was asking ten euros for an antique lamp.
"Five euros?" I suggested.
"Eight," he replied.
"Seven, and I'll tell you its story." Sold!
The lamp came from his grandfather's café.
At noon, I went home with my treasures: the book, the lamp, and a nearly new sweater for two euros.
Tonight, the lamp is on my desk.
A new object has no story.
An old object has a thousand.
That's why I love flea markets.

sentences: For ten years, Thomas worked the same job: an accountant in a large company.
The salary was good, the job was stable, but he was bored.
Every day, the same tasks, the same routine.
One morning, he realized that he no longer wanted to get up to go to work.
Changing careers after thirty-five is not easy.
It's even a real risk.
Thomas was earning a good living; by changing, he might earn less, at least at first.
"You're crazy," some colleagues told him.
But others encouraged him: "At least you're trying."
Thomas had dreamed for a long time of working with wood.
So he decided to retrain and become a carpenter.
To do this, he took a course for a year.
Going back to school at his age, with younger students, required courage.
But he dared.
Today, Thomas earns a little less money than before, and his days are more physically tiring.
Yet, he has never been so happy.
In the evening, he looks at the furniture he has made with his own hands, and he feels a real pride.
Of course, retraining is not possible for everyone, and it doesn't always succeed.
But Thomas's story raises a good question: is it better to have a comfortable job that bores us, or a more challenging job that has meaning for us?

sentences: In France, people drink coffee.
In England, people drink tea.
It's a small difference, but it says a lot.
French coffee is small and strong.
It's called an 'espresso.'
It's drunk quickly, standing, at the counter.
It takes two minutes.

They drink their coffee and go to work.
Coffee costs less at the counter than at a table.

We talk.

sentences: Two years ago, I almost quit my job.
Today, I'm happy I stayed.
At that time, I was unhappy.
I was working a lot, but I didn't see the results.
My team was small and we had too many projects.
Every evening, I came home exhausted.
One Monday morning, I made my decision.
I wrote a resignation letter and printed it.
I wanted to give it to my boss in the afternoon.
But during lunch, I talked with a colleague, Aïcha.
She had been working at the company for twelve years.
I explained everything to her.
She listened without interrupting me.
Then she said to me: 'I understand.
But have you talked to your boss about the problem?'
I thought about it.
No.
I had never said anything.
I thought it was useless.
So, that afternoon, I went to see my boss.
But I didn't give her my letter.
Instead, I explained the situation honestly.
She was surprised.
'Why didn't you talk to me earlier?'
We talked for an hour.
Two weeks later, she hired one more person for my team.
Today, I enjoy my job again.
I kept the letter in a drawer.
It reminds me of a lesson: you have to speak up before leaving.

I looked at the paper for five minutes.

sentences: My brother Thomas smoked for twenty years.
He started at sixteen and he smoked about a pack a day.
He had already tried to quit four times.
Each time, he lasted two or three weeks, then he started again.
Last year, something changed.
Our father had a heart problem and he spent a week in the hospital.
Thomas was silent for a long time after that visit.
Then he told me, 'This time, I'm quitting for good.'
But he did one thing differently: he asked for help.
Before, he always tried alone.
He went to see his doctor, who offered him patches.
He also joined a group of people who were quitting at the same time.
The first weeks were very hard.
He was nervous, he slept poorly.
He called me several times in the evening, just to talk.
He also changed his habits.
Before, he always smoked with his morning coffee, so he stopped having his coffee in the same place.
After a month, it was easier.
After three months, he was going up the stairs without being out of breath.
It's now been fourteen months.
He told me recently, 'The first four times, I tried alone.
The fifth time, I accepted to be helped.'

sentences: For two years, I've been working from home three days a week.
On Tuesdays and Thursdays, I go to the office.
At first, I was very happy.
No more commuting: I was saving an hour and a half each day.
I could sleep a little longer.
I also noticed that I worked better on certain tasks.
At the office, people interrupted me all the time.
At home, I could concentrate without being disturbed.
But after a few months, problems appeared.
The first problem was space.
My apartment is small.
I worked at the kitchen table, the same table where I ate in the evening.
The second problem was time.
Without commuting, there was no clear limit anymore.
I started at eight o'clock and was still checking my messages at nine o'clock.
The third problem was loneliness.
Some days, I didn't talk to anyone face to face.
So I changed several things.
I bought a small second-hand desk to separate work from meals.
Now I do a 'fake outing': I walk for twenty minutes before starting and twenty minutes at the end.
Remote work is neither good nor bad.
It all depends on the rules you set for yourself.

sentences: One day, I will leave the city. Many city dwellers say this.
Some actually do it.
It's interesting to listen to what they say afterwards.
The reasons for leaving often look similar: the cost of housing, fatigue, noise, the desire for a garden, and sometimes the birth of a child.
The possibility of remote work has made this project realistic for people who, in the past, wouldn't have been able to consider it.
Those who succeed in their move almost always mention the same factors.
First, they chose a place they already knew, where they had family or friends.
Arriving somewhere without knowing anyone is much more difficult than one might think.
Then, they checked the practical aspects before leaving: internet coverage, the distance to school, the doctor, and the supermarket.
These details seem secondary from an apartment in the city; they shape daily life in the countryside.
Finally, they got involved in local life — the sports club, the events committee, the school.
Those who stay among themselves, without ever participating, often feel isolated after a year.
Those who return to the city mention three things: isolation, dependence on the car for even the smallest trips, and their teenagers' boredom.
So there isn't a universally correct answer.
The real question isn't 'city or countryside?', but 'what am I fleeing from, and what am I looking for?'.
Those who leave just to escape are rarely satisfied.

sentences: It's easy to blame yourself for your lack of willpower in front of a phone.
This forgets that these apps are designed, by entire teams, to capture attention for as long as possible.
The main mechanism has a name: variable reward.
When you pull down the news feed, you don't know what you're going to find — nothing interesting, or something exciting.
This uncertainty is exactly the principle of slot machines, and the brain reacts very strongly to it.
A predictable reward becomes boring; an unpredictable reward keeps you engaged.
Other elements are added: infinite scrolling, which removes any natural stopping point; the automatic playback of the next video; notifications, which create an interruption that's hard to ignore.
None of these techniques are an accident.
They are measured, tested, optimized.
The result is measurable: the average screen time exceeds three hours a day in most European countries.
It's not just three hours wasted, because part of it is useful.
But very few people, when honestly asked, say they chose this time.
What to do?
The effective advice doesn't rely on willpower, but on friction.
Turning off non-essential notifications removes interruptions.
Putting the most captivating apps in a folder, out of the home screen, adds two gestures — which is often enough.
Leaving the phone in another room at night is more effective than any resolution.
The idea is not to demonize these tools, which provide immense services.
It's to restore a more balanced relationship: that we decide when to engage, not the other way around.

sentences: In France, about one in three households consists of a single person.
This proportion has doubled in fifty years, and it continues to rise.
This figure is often commented on in a worried tone.
It deserves to be examined more calmly, as it mixes two different realities.
Living alone is a housing situation.
It is sometimes chosen and appreciated: freedom, calm, absence of daily compromises.
Many people living alone have a rich social life.
Isolation is something else.
It is the absence of regular relationships and support, and it can perfectly exist within a couple or a family.
This distinction is important because the documented health effects concern isolation, not the fact of living alone.
Research is quite convergent: prolonged isolation increases cardiovascular risks, promotes depression, and in some studies, compares to well-known risk factors like smoking.
The most affected populations are not always those we imagine.
Widowed elderly people, yes.
But also young adults who have just arrived in a city, and caregivers who look after a sick relative and have no time for themselves.
Effective responses do not consist of telling people to 'go out more.'
They create opportunities: associations, neighborhood activities, community gardens, third places, organized visits.
What makes these initiatives effective is regularity.
A one-time event is not enough.
Living alone is therefore neither good nor bad in itself.
What matters is the number of people who would notice your absence.

sentences: Reading is credited with many virtues: it would make you more intelligent, more empathetic, and more focused.
These claims deserve to be examined separately, as they are not based on the same evidence.
The most established effect concerns vocabulary.
People who read a lot have a significantly larger vocabulary, and this link is strong.
The reason is simple: written language contains words that everyday conversation almost never uses.
You can go through life without ever hearing certain terms that a novel naturally uses.
However, vocabulary is not just an ornament.
It determines the ability to understand a complex text, a contract, a medical article, or a public debate.
The second effect, which is more debated, concerns empathy.
Several studies suggest that reading fiction improves the ability to perceive the mental states of others.
The results are real but fragile, and the nature of the relationship remains uncertain: more empathetic people may read more novels, rather than the other way around.
The third effect is the most interesting in our time: concentration.
Reading a long text requires maintaining attention without immediate reward, while keeping in mind what has come before.
It is an exercise that has become rare.
Most of our daily readings are brief and interrupted.
This is not about nostalgia: there is no proof that a novel is better than a good article.
What matters is the duration of continuous attention.
So, does reading make you more intelligent?
The question is poorly posed.
It develops a capacity that few other activities still cultivate.

sentences: Every year, many amateur athletes get injured.
Contrary to what one might think, most of these injuries are not the result of an accident: they are what are called 'overuse' injuries, which develop gradually.
The pattern is almost always the same.

A person returns to sports with enthusiasm, quickly increases the duration or intensity, and after a few weeks feels a pain that they initially ignore, which then forces them to stop for several months.
The explanation lies in a difference in pace between the body's tissues.
The cardiovascular system adapts quickly: within a few weeks, one is noticeably less out of breath.
The muscles also adapt fairly quickly.
But tendons, ligaments, and bones adapt much more slowly, over several months.
The danger comes precisely from this gap.
One feels capable of doing more long before the structures that absorb the shock are ready.
Hence the rule often cited by physiotherapists: increase the load by about ten percent per week at most, and regularly plan for a lighter week.
Two other factors constantly come up.
The first is sleep: it is during rest that repair occurs.
Training a lot while sleeping little is an excellent way to get injured.
The second is variety.
Repeating exactly the same movement always stresses the same tissues.
Alternating activities distributes the strain.
Finally, a pain that lasts more than a few days deserves attention, not patience.
Most long-term injuries started with a discomfort that was chosen to be ignored.

sentences: Light pollution is a relatively recent issue that was long considered secondary.
Research conducted over the past twenty years has changed this perspective.
Artificial night lighting has significantly increased worldwide, and nearly the entire European population now lives under a sky where the Milky Way is invisible.
The documented effects concern a large part of living beings.
For insects, light acts like a trap.
They circle around light sources until exhaustion, do not reproduce, and become easy prey.
It is estimated that night lighting is among the causes of the decline in insect populations.
For migratory birds, which navigate partly by the stars, illuminated cities are disorienting.
Collisions with lit buildings are regularly observed.
Bats, which hunt at night, avoid lit areas and thus lose hunting territories.
Plants themselves are affected: trees located under streetlights keep their leaves longer in autumn.
In humans, night light disrupts melatonin production and sleep quality.
What makes this issue particular is that it is easy to correct — much more so than most environmental problems.
Turning off a light requires neither technology nor heavy investment.
It even reduces the bill.
Many French municipalities have already implemented a midnight light-out policy, with no increase in crime observed, contrary to expressed fears.
Few ecological measures are cheaper and act as quickly.
It literally just takes pressing a switch.

sentences: Antibiotics are among the most important medical discoveries of the twentieth century.
Before them, a common infection could be deadly.
However, they suffer from a persistent misunderstanding: many people see them as a general remedy for being sick.
An antibiotic works against bacteria.
It has absolutely no effect on a virus.
This means it is useless against the flu, the cold, or most sore throats and bronchitis, which are of viral origin.
Taking an antibiotic in these cases does not speed up recovery by a single day.
This raises two problems.
The first is individual: antibiotics have side effects, particularly on the intestinal flora, and it is absurd to endure them without benefit.
The second is collective, and it is much more serious.
Every unnecessary use promotes the emergence of resistant bacteria.
The mechanism is simple: the bacteria that survive the treatment are precisely those that resist it, and they are the ones that then multiply.
Antibiotic resistance is now considered by health authorities to be one of the main long-term threats.
Infections that were once easy to treat are becoming difficult again.
That is why campaigns regularly remind us that antibiotics are not automatic, and why it is important to complete a prescribed treatment rather than stopping as soon as you feel better.
It should also be recognized that the pressure does not come solely from patients.
A rushed doctor, faced with someone who insists, sometimes prescribes to avoid conflict.
The right question to ask is not 'Can you give me something?', but 'Is it viral?'.

sentences: Few school subjects are as divisive as homework.
Some see it as a way to teach personal responsibility; others see it as a source of inequality and family tension.
Research on the topic allows us to move beyond the certainties of both sides, provided we distinguish by age.
For elementary school students, studies show no significant effect of homework on results.
A young child primarily learns in class and through play; adding homework doesn't contribute much and can even harm their relationship with school if it leads to evening conflicts.
For older students, however, a positive effect appears, as long as the homework remains reasonable in duration.
Beyond a certain threshold, the benefit disappears, or even reverses.
But the strongest argument against homework is not its ineffectiveness: it's its impact on inequality.
A homework assignment implicitly assumes a supportive environment: a quiet place, an adult available to help, and sometimes material resources.
These conditions are not equally distributed.
Two children receiving the same assignment are therefore not in the same situation.
That's why many schools have developed after-school homework assistance programs, specifically to restore this equality.
The debate, at its core, is less about the homework itself than about what is expected of families.
A system that relies heavily on homework assumes families that are available and equipped.
Not all families are, and that's where the principle of equality truly comes into play.

sentences: Many people imagine history as a set of facts that are established once and for all.
The reality is different: the history taught evolves, and this evolution is not a flaw, but a sign of a living discipline.
This change has several sources.
The first is the discovery of new sources.
Archives are opening after decades of closure; documents are reappearing; techniques are advancing, allowing us to date or analyze what could not be examined before.
The second, deeper source is the change in the questions being asked.
For a long time, history focused on kings, battles, and great men.
In the twentieth century, historians began to take an interest in the lives of ordinary people: how they ate, worked, and died.
This history of daily life did not exist before we decided to seek it out.
More recently, other voices have been included: those of women, largely absent from ancient narratives, those of the colonized, and those of the defeated.
This process is sometimes misunderstood.
It is seen as a suspicious 'rewriting,' as if the past were being manipulated.
This confuses two things.
Falsifying facts is a wrongdoing.
Asking new questions about the same facts is the normal work of the discipline.
An example: the facts of colonial conquest are widely known.
But telling them from the perspective of the colonizers or that of the colonized gives two different stories, both based on sources.
History is therefore never entirely neutral.
What makes it reliable is not the absence of perspective.
It is the method, and the possibility of verification.

sentences: Holding a door, greeting the driver, letting someone pass, nodding in thanks: these gestures may seem insignificant.
However, they actually play a more important role than we think in the quality of communal life.
Researchers who study daily life sometimes refer to these gestures as 'micro-interactions.'
Taken individually, they don't weigh much.
When multiplied by thousands each day, they shape the atmosphere of a city or neighborhood.
Their function is not only practical.
Saying hello to a shopkeeper isn't about exchanging information: it's about recognizing each other as people.
It's a minimal but real signal: 'I see you, you matter.'
The absence of these gestures is immediately noticeable.
In a place where no one says hello, where everyone looks at their phone, a diffuse tension sets in, hard to name.
These courtesies have another effect, one that can be measured: they spread.
A gesture of courtesy increases the likelihood that the person who benefits from it will do one in return.
Conversely, rudeness is contagious: someone who is poorly received tends to receive others poorly afterward.
We must avoid two extremes.
The first would be to idealize a past that was necessarily more polite — every generation wrongly believes that politeness is declining.
The second would be to dismiss these gestures as superficial.
They don't solve any major problems.
But they make it bearable to live with millions of others in the same place.
A society is not only made up of laws.
It is also made up of hellos.

sentences: For four years, I've been living without a car.
When I say this, the reactions are extreme: some find it admirable, others unimaginable.
Both are partly wrong, because it all depends on where you live.
In my case, it wasn't a heroic ecological sacrifice.
It was a calculation.
I tallied up what my car was costing me: the purchase, insurance, maintenance, fuel, and parking.
The annual total surprised me.
I live in a city where the bus, bike, and walking are sufficient for most needs, and where you can rent a car on the rare occasions when it's necessary.
The calculation was quick: keeping a car that I used three times a month didn't make sense.
The benefits outweighed the costs.
Walking and biking every day effortlessly replaced the exercise I never found time for.
I know my city better.
And I discovered an unexpected relief: no longer searching for parking, no longer thinking about the technical inspection, no longer enduring traffic jams.
But I refrain from making it a general lesson.
This choice is only possible because of my situation: a dense city, well-served, with a job nearby.
For a family in a rural area, without transportation, with long commutes and children to drive, a car is not a luxury: it's a necessity.
To blame these people would be unfair and absurd.
The real question is therefore not individual but collective.
It is not 'why do you keep a car?'.
It is: how many people today have no other choice, and what are we doing about it?

sentences: In France, millions of people regularly give their time, unpaid, to associations: sports, food aid, tutoring, emergency services, culture, and the environment.
This phenomenon raises an interesting question.
Why dedicate precious time to strangers, without payment?
The answer 'out of kindness' is too simple and a bit false.
Research on volunteering shows multiple motivations, often mixed, and not always selfless — which is not surprising.
Of course, there is the desire to be useful, to contribute to something greater than oneself.
This is real, and it is important.
But there are also more personal motivations that volunteers readily acknowledge.
Social connection, first.
Many people become volunteers at a time of solitude: after retirement, a move, or a bereavement.
The association provides them with a framework, meetings, and a role.
Meaning comes next.
A paid job does not always provide the feeling of being useful.
Volunteering sometimes fills this gap.
Learning as well.
You develop skills, meet different environments, and break out of your routine.
Interestingly, studies show that regular volunteering is associated with better well-being and even better health.
Giving your time also benefits the giver.
Understanding these motivations does not diminish the value of the act.
On the contrary.
This means that volunteering is not reserved for saints.
It is an ordinary human activity that meets needs on both sides.
Which is rather good news.
What benefits the helper lasts longer.

sentences: The history of work is also a history of disappearances.
Professions that were once widespread have faded away, rendered useless by an invention, a machine, or a change in usage.
Lamp lighters, telephone operators, typesetters: these professions, which employed many, hardly exist anymore.
And the trend continues, affecting today professions that were thought to be safe.
This phenomenon is generally analyzed in economic terms: jobs destroyed, others created, a balance to measure.
This approach is necessary, but it overlooks a more personal dimension.
A profession is not just a source of income; it is a skill, a pride, a place in the world.
When it disappears, it is not just a salary that vanishes, but an identity.
Let’s take the example of a craftsman whose skill, passed down through generations, suddenly becomes irrelevant.

Even if he finds another job, something has been lost that no retraining can replace: the mastery painstakingly acquired, the recognition that accompanied it, the feeling of belonging to a lineage of people who did the same thing.
In short, he is asked to give up not just a task, but a part of himself.
It would be futile to try to freeze the world to preserve every profession.
Technological progress, on the whole, has freed humans from arduous work, and very few would sincerely regret going back down the mine.
Refusing all change in the name of threatened jobs would mean condemning future generations to a perpetual present.
But recognizing the necessity of change does not mean ignoring the human cost.

A society that accepts the disappearance of professions should, in return, support those who practiced them — not just with a simple compensation, but with real means to rebuild their place and dignity.
For behind every profession that fades away, there are people who had learned to be proud of it.
To forget this is to treat as a mere statistic what is, for them, a deep wound.

sentences: Noise may be the most underestimated form of pollution in urban life.
Traffic, construction sites, sirens, machines, amplified voices: the city produces a constant background noise that we eventually stop paying attention to.
Not that it has disappeared, but because we have gotten used to it.
However, this habit is deceptive: even when we no longer listen to it, noise continues to affect us.
Research on this topic is compelling.
Prolonged exposure to noise not only causes temporary discomfort; it affects sleep, raises tension, and maintains a state of stress of which we are not even aware.
The body reacts to the din even if the mind believes it is ignoring it.
Silence is therefore not just a luxury for sensitive souls; it is a condition of health, just like air or water.
The problem is that silence, in our cities, has become an unevenly distributed luxury.
Those who can afford it settle in quiet neighborhoods, soundproof their homes, and escape on weekends to peaceful places.
The others endure, with no escape, the continuous rumble of major roads and poorly soundproofed housing.
Calm, once available to everyone, is thus tending to become a privilege that money can buy.
Restoring a place for silence in the city is, however, not out of reach.
This involves concrete choices: limiting speed and thus noise from traffic, greening the streets, creating calm zones, and demanding better sound insulation for homes.
None of these measures are spectacular, but their cumulative effect would profoundly transform the daily experience of millions of residents.
We must especially stop viewing noise as an inevitability of urban life, a nuisance to which we should simply adapt.
The din is not an unavoidable characteristic of cities; it is the result of choices—of planning, transport, construction—that other choices could correct.
Demanding silence is not fleeing the city or dreaming of an impossible countryside calm.
It is asking that urban life, so dense and vibrant, also allows for spaces where we can finally hear ourselves think.

sentences: Technology is neutral; it all depends on how we use it." This phrase, repeated a thousand times, has a reassuring quality: it places the responsibility entirely on the user and absolves the tool itself.
A knife can cut bread or harm; it is not the knife that decides.
The idea seems sensible.
However, upon closer inspection, it is largely insufficient.
For while every technology allows for multiple uses, it does not allow them all equally.
Each tool makes some actions easy and others difficult; it inclines, it directs, it suggests.
A car does not force anyone to drive fast, but it makes speed possible and desirable in a way that a bicycle does not.
A social network does not compel anyone to compare themselves to others, but it is designed in such a way that comparison becomes almost inevitable.
The tool does not decide for us, but it is also not indifferent to what we do with it.
We can go further.
Some technologies carry effects within them that go beyond any individual use.
The automobile, by becoming widespread, did not just transport people: it reshaped cities, dispersed living spaces, transformed our lifestyles.
No one had decided this; it is the tool itself that, by its own logic, has shaped the world around it.
To claim it was 'neutral' is to ignore this power of transformation.
Recognizing this does not mean holding technology responsible for everything, nor does it absolve individuals.
We remain free in our uses, and this freedom is real.
But it operates within a framework that the tool has already, in part, set up.
Ignoring this framework is to believe oneself freer than one is, and to become blind to the forces that shape our behaviors.
The issue is important, as it concerns how we conceive of technologies themselves.
If we accept that they are not neutral, then it becomes legitimate to ask, even before adopting them, what uses they favor and what effects they produce.
The question is no longer just 'how will I use it?', but 'what will this tool do to me, and to us?'.
Believing technology is neutral is to give up judging it.
However, the tools we give ourselves shape us in return, and it is better to know this before they change us.

sentences: From childhood, we are taught to fear mistakes.
At school, it is punished with a bad grade; in life, it is a source of shame.
We come to see it as a failure, something to be avoided at all costs.
However, this view, as widespread as it may be, is based on a deep misunderstanding.
Far from being just the enemy of learning, mistakes are often its very condition.
Let's think about how we actually learn anything.
We try, we make mistakes, we understand why, we correct, we start again.
The child learning to walk falls countless times; the one learning a language makes mistakes before speaking correctly.
At no point are these mistakes failures: they are the necessary steps of progress.
Without them, no real learning would be possible, because it is precisely by confronting our limits that we push them back.
Research confirms this intuition.
We learn better and more durably when we have first fumbled, struggled, and failed, than when we passively receive a ready-made solution.
The effort that precedes the mistake, and the understanding that follows its correction, engraves knowledge much more deeply than a lesson absorbed without difficulty.
Mistakes are not a regrettable accident on the path; they are the path itself.
So why do we fear them so much?
Because we have been shaped by a culture that punishes them instead of exploiting them.
By punishing mistakes rather than using them, we teach people not to stop making them, but to be afraid to try.
However, those who fear making mistakes dare less, try less, and ultimately learn less.
The fear of mistakes thus produces the exact opposite of what it claims to achieve.
Changing our relationship with mistakes would have considerable effects, far beyond school.
In work, in creation, in research, advances almost always arise from a succession of overcome failures.
Environments that allow mistakes, that treat them as information rather than faults, are those where the most invention and progress occur.
Conversely, the fear of making mistakes sterilizes.
It is not about celebrating mistakes for their own sake, nor about being satisfied with our faults.
It is about stopping the demonization of mistakes, to see what they really are: not the failure of learning, but its most faithful instrument.
Those who never accept making mistakes condemn themselves, in reality, to never truly learn.

sentences: We commonly judge the value of something by its price.
What is expensive seems precious to us, while what is cheap seems advantageous.
This convenient reflex, however, rests on a confusion: the price of something does not reflect its true cost.
Often, the displayed price reflects only a part of what the item truly cost, with the rest being borne by others, elsewhere, without appearing on the receipt.
Let's take a product sold at a very low price.
This attractive price can hide very real but invisible costs: underpaid workers who made it, an environment degraded by its production, depleted resources, and damages deferred to the future.
These costs exist; it's just that the buyer does not pay them directly.
Economists talk about 'externalized' costs: pushed outside the price, borne by society, by nature, by future generations.
A low price is therefore not a true saving; it is a shifting of the cost onto those who cannot defend themselves.
Conversely, a high price does not guarantee that something is truly 'worth' what it costs.
A portion of the price may not compensate for quality, but for an image, a brand, or artificial scarcity.
Paying a high price does not always mean paying for value; sometimes it is paying for prestige, or simply for the satisfaction of having paid a lot.
The price, indeed, is a misleading guide.
Understanding this transforms the way we view consumption.
It invites us to ask, behind each price, what the real cost is: who produced it, under what conditions, and with what consequences?
These questions do not always have easy answers, and we cannot investigate every purchase.
But just having these questions in mind is enough to make us less naive, less quick to confuse cheapness with advantage.
This awareness also has a collective significance.
If prices told the truth — if they included the costs currently externalized — many harmful products would be more expensive, and many virtuous products would be more competitive.
Ensuring that prices reflect real costs is one of the major challenges of a fairer and more sustainable economy, even if it faces immense resistance.
The price is therefore only partial information, and sometimes misleading.
Behind the displayed figures lies a more complex reality that is worth learning to see.
For what we do not pay, someone, somewhere, pays on our behalf.

sentences: Chance exists, but our minds struggle to accept it.
When faced with events that are purely due to chance, we stubbornly seek meaning, a cause, or an intention.
We see shapes in the cloud of coincidences, signs in what is merely random, and trends in what is just fluctuation.

This difficulty in accepting chance, in recognizing it for what it is, is not trivial: it distorts our judgment in a thousand ways, and understanding chance is one of the most useful and counterintuitive things that reason can learn.
Where does this resistance come from?
Surely from a deep tendency to seek explanations everywhere.
Seeing causes and intentions has been an advantage for our ancestors: it was better to imagine a predator behind a noise than to ignore a real danger.
This reflex, valuable in the face of threats, misleads us when it comes to chance: it makes us attribute meaning to what has none, to discern a will where there are only coincidences.
We are, in a way, wired to reject chance.
This refusal produces characteristic errors.
After a series of coincidences, we believe in a link that does not exist.
In the face of a sequence of results, we imagine a regularity, a 'series', where only chance operates.
We are surprised by coincidences that, statistically, were almost certain to occur one day, given such a large number of occasions.
We draw conclusions from a small number of cases, forgetting that a small sample fluctuates greatly.
All these errors have a common root: our inability to conceive what chance actually produces.
Understanding chance, then, is first and foremost about accepting a disturbing idea: many things happen without reason, without a determined cause, without intention.
A striking coincidence may be just a coincidence; a success or a failure may owe much to chance; a series may have no meaning.
Recognizing the role of chance does not mean giving up on understanding the world; it means understanding that a part of the world inherently escapes any explanation in terms of causes or intentions.
This understanding has concrete virtues.
It makes us more cautious in the face of coincidences, more modest in our successes as well as our failures, and more resistant to the illusions that exploit our difficulty with chance.
It protects against those who, playing on this tendency, sell us imaginary causes, miracle remedies, and misleading explanations of what is merely fluctuation.
Knowing how to recognize chance is to safeguard oneself against a host of errors and manipulations.
Finally, understanding chance is a form of wisdom.
It is accepting that we do not control everything, that chance plays a role in our lives that we prefer to ignore, that not everything has a hidden meaning.
This clarity may seem austere; it is also liberating.
For recognizing the role of chance is to stop desperately searching for meaning where there is none, and to focus our intelligence where it can truly understand.

sentences: We tend to oppose two terms as if they referred to two distinct worlds: on one side, 'man', and on the other, 'nature'.
We talk about protecting nature, about returning to nature, as if it were an external domain, separate from us.
This way of thinking is so deeply ingrained that it seems obvious to us.
However, upon examination, this separation proves problematic, and it is not certain that it serves us well.
For in what sense would we be separated from nature?
We are living beings, made of the same matter as the rest of the living world, subject to the same biological laws, depending at every moment on air, water, and other species.
Our body is nature; our existence is woven into the web of life.
We do not hover above nature as a separate kingdom; we are a part of it, as integrally as a tree or an animal.
The opposition between man and nature contradicts this elementary fact.
Where does this stubborn separation come from, then?
From several sources.
From a long tradition that has placed man above the rest of creation, endowed with a soul or reason that would radically distinguish him.
From the development of cities, which has distanced most of us from daily contact with the living world, to the point of perceiving it as something other.
From our technical power, finally, which has given us the illusion of dominating nature, thus making us feel external to and superior over it.
This separation is a historical construct, not a given.
However, this construct is not without consequences, and many of them are unfortunate.

By thinking of ourselves as outside of nature, we have been able to treat it as a mere backdrop, a reservoir of resources to exploit without limit, without realizing that by degrading it, we are harming ourselves.
The ecological crisis is, in a sense, the repressed return of this separation: we are suddenly discovering that we were not outside, that what we inflict on nature, we inflict on ourselves.
One does not saw off the branch on which one is sitting, believing it belongs to another tree.
Should we then deny any difference between humans and the rest of the living world?
That would be an opposite excess.
We have unique capabilities — language, reflection, culture, an unparalleled power to act — which make us distinct beings, not by a separate nature, but by increased responsibility.
Recognizing our belonging to nature does not erase our specificity; it gives it its true meaning: not one of domination, but one of responsibility towards a world of which we are a part.
Rethinking our relationship with nature therefore requires overcoming the separation that has made us strangers to it.

Not to dissolve ourselves in it, nor to renounce what distinguishes us, but to recognize ourselves as what we are: a part of the living world, unique and responsible, whose fate is linked to that of the whole.
Knowing ourselves to be in nature, and not above it, may be the first step towards a more just relationship with the world.

sentences: An idea that has long been marginal is now entering the public debate: providing every citizen, unconditionally and without compensation, a guaranteed income sufficient to live.
This 'universal income' evokes passionate reactions, with some seeing it as a dangerous utopia and others considering it a necessity for the future.
Beyond the slogans, the idea deserves serious examination, as it touches on fundamental questions about work, dignity, and solidarity.
The arguments in its favor are of several kinds.
The first is related to automation: if machines permanently destroy a part of jobs, how can we ensure an income for those who will no longer find work?
A guaranteed income would provide an answer by disconnecting survival from employment.

The second argument is about dignity: by ensuring everyone a minimum unconditionally, we would eliminate the fear of tomorrow and free individuals from the constraint of having to accept any job under any conditions.
The third is about simplicity: a universal income would replace the complicated and sometimes humiliating maze of existing aids.
But the objections are no less serious.
The first is the cost: providing everyone with a sufficient income would represent a colossal sum, the financing of which raises immense difficulties.
The second relates to work: if everyone receives enough to live without working, some fear a collapse of activity, a society where production would cease.
The third is moral: is it fair to provide an income to those who could work and choose not to, risking placing the burden of their idleness on others?
These objections deserve to be taken seriously, but some are based on questionable assumptions.

The idea that people would massively stop working if they received a basic income is not confirmed by experiments conducted here and there: most continue to work, but with more freedom in their choices.

As for the fear of widespread idleness, it is based on a pessimistic view of human beings, assumed to work only under the constraint of need—a view contradicted by the widespread desire to be active and useful.
The question of financing, however, remains real, and it cannot be brushed aside.
A generous universal income would require a profound overhaul of taxation and social protection, with consequences that are difficult to predict.
That is why the debate often focuses less on the principle than on the modalities: what amount, financed how, in replacement of what.
A modest income does not have the same effects as a sufficient income to live, and one can support the idea in one version and reject it in another.

Whether one is for or against it, the debate on universal income has the merit of raising a question that the future may make unavoidable: in a society where work may no longer be enough to occupy and sustain everyone, how can we guarantee everyone a dignified existence?
The answer is not obvious, but the question itself will not be easily evaded for long.

sentences: Every day, without thinking about it, we produce an immense amount of data: what we search for, buy, watch, where we go, and who we talk to.
Taken in isolation, these traces seem insignificant.
When gathered and analyzed, they represent one of the most coveted resources of our time.
A considerable economy has been built around them, which has made the fortune of some of the most powerful companies in the world.
Understanding this economy means understanding what we give up without realizing it.
These data are worth gold for a specific reason: they allow us to predict and influence behaviors.
By analyzing our traces, we can guess our tastes, needs, weaknesses, and moments of vulnerability.
We can then send the message that is most likely to make us act — to buy, click, or sometimes vote — at the right moment.
Our data not only serve to know us; they serve to act upon us, with greater precision as they become more numerous and better analyzed.
The market that has formed on this basis is largely invisible to those who feed it, namely us.
We provide the raw material — our traces — without perceiving their value, in exchange for services that seem free to us.
But nothing is free: what we do not pay for in money, we pay for in data, and this data is often worth much more than the service received.
In this economy, we are less customers than the product sold to others: advertisers, to whom access to our attention and knowledge of our behaviors is resold.
This system raises questions that go beyond mere privacy.
First, a question of fairness: is it fair that the value created by our data benefits almost entirely those who collect it, without us gaining anything, or even being aware of it?
Then, a question of power: the accumulation of this data gives a few companies unprecedented knowledge and influence, which largely escapes democratic control.
Those who know everything about us hold a power over us that no one has ever had.
In the face of this situation, several responses are emerging.
Some advocate for a return to individual control: that everyone should know what data is collected, oppose it, or even profit from it.
Others believe that the response can only be collective and political: to strictly regulate data collection, limit what can be done with the data, and break the concentration of this power.
The two paths are not mutually exclusive, and both assume first a raising of awareness: that what we give up so lightly has immense value.
Our data is worth gold, but others are the ones collecting it.
Becoming aware of this reality is not giving in to paranoia; it is stopping being naive.
What we leave behind us, day after day, is not without consequence: it is the material of a power that is exercised over us, and it would be better to face it than to continue ignoring it.

sentences: It is often believed that the main danger of misinformation is that it makes us believe falsehoods.
This is a real danger, but there is another, more insidious and perhaps more serious one: that it makes us doubt everything, to the point of believing nothing at all.

Because after discovering that certain information was false, that certain sources lied, and that certain authorities were mistaken, we can slip into a generalized skepticism where nothing is worthy of trust.
And this total skepticism is, in its own way, as dangerous as gullibility.
This shift has a logic to it.
Deceived multiple times, we become distrustful, which is healthy.

But this distrust, if it doesn't stop, turns into a general mistrust of everything: all media would lie, all experts would be biased, no institution would be reliable, and all information would be suspect.
At this stage, we can no longer distinguish the reliable from the dubious; we reject everything outright, convinced that we cannot trust anything or anyone.
Legitimate doubt has turned into absolute cynicism.
However, this cynicism, far from protecting against manipulation, exposes us even more.
For the one who believes nothing does not believe in nothing: they end up believing anything, or rather what suits them, what flatters their prejudices, what comes from their own camp.
Having rejected all reliable sources in the name of distrust, they find themselves without a reference point, at the mercy of the first discourse that can exploit their resentment.
Total skepticism does not lead to clarity, but to a new gullibility, more dangerous because it believes itself to be critical.
There is more.
A society where no one believes anything becomes ungovernable in the deepest sense: it loses the very ability to agree on common facts.
However, a democracy, a debate, a collective decision assumes that we can start from shared facts, recognized by all.
If everyone has their own 'facts', if no truth is common anymore, there is no longer any possible debate, only opposing camps without common ground.
The destruction of trust in any shared truth undermines the very foundations of communal life.
That is why those who seek to manipulate sometimes have less interest in making us believe a specific thing than in destroying our trust in any truth.

Sowing doubt everywhere, blurring the lines between true and false, making us believe that 'in any case, we can know nothing': this strategy of generalized doubt is formidable because it disarms resistance.
A people that believes nothing can no longer be outraged by anything, nor unite around anything.
Cynicism is the best ally of lies.
The right attitude is therefore neither gullibility, which believes everything, nor cynicism, which believes nothing, but a measured skepticism that knows how to distinguish.
To doubt, yes, but with discernment; to be wary, but without rejecting everything outright; to recognize that one can be deceived, without concluding that one can never know anything.
To preserve the ability to believe what deserves it, while being wary of what does not deserve it: this is the difficult but vital balance that a world saturated with falsehoods requires.

sentences: At the end of this reflection on connection and solitude, a truth emerges, confirmed by both common experience and research: in the face of life's challenges, what protects us best is not primarily material wealth or even individual strength, but other people.
Social connection, the presence of people we can rely on, is one of the most precious resources in life — and one of the most neglected.
Studies on well-being and health are remarkably convergent on this point.

The quality of a person's relationships — the depth of their connections, the presence of loved ones, the feeling of being supported — is among the most determining factors of their happiness, resilience in the face of challenges, and even their physical health and longevity.
Those who are surrounded cope better with difficulties, heal better, and live longer.
Connection is not just a source of joy; it is a true protection, as concrete as it is invisible.
It's easy to see why.

In the face of a challenge — an illness, a bereavement, a loss, a difficulty — the person who is alone faces it with all their strength, which is often insufficient; the person who is surrounded can lean on others, be supported, helped, and comforted.
Others provide material help, but especially that moral support that allows one to endure: the feeling of not being alone, of being carried, of mattering to someone.
A shared challenge is lighter than a solitary one, not because it changes in nature, but because it is no longer borne alone.
This strength of connection also applies at the level of communities and societies.
In the face of disasters, crises, and collective misfortunes, it is the most supportive societies, where the bonds are strongest, that withstand the best.
Where everyone is alone, the crisis dislocates; where people are connected, they help each other, support each other, and hold together.

The strength of a society is not only measured by its wealth or power, but by the quality of the bonds that unite its members, by their ability to face challenges together rather than each for themselves.
This observation should alert us, because we live in societies that, as we have seen, tend to break down connections: individualism, mobility, screens, and the disappearance of meeting places.
By weakening what connects us, we also weaken, often without realizing it, our collective and individual protection in the face of challenges.
We gain autonomy and freedom, but we lose resilience, support, and shared strength.
A society of isolated individuals is a more fragile society, where everyone is more exposed.
Recognizing that connection is strength means understanding that maintaining relationships, weaving and preserving bonds, is not a mere luxury, but an essential investment.

The time spent on others, the attention given to loved ones, the commitment to a community, is never time wasted: it builds the net that will support us in challenges, and that we will extend, in turn, under others.
In a world that exalts the autonomous individual, it is worth remembering this ancient truth: that our greatest strength, in the face of life's fragility, is each other.

sentences: We take debate for granted, almost as a natural backdrop of democratic life.
We forget that it is actually a late and precarious achievement, resting on such demanding conditions that it is more surprising that it exists than that it is fragile.

For debating, in the fullest sense, does not mean merely allowing opposing opinions to coexist in the same space; it means accepting to subject one's convictions to the test of contradiction, in the hope that something more true or more just will emerge.
Such a disposition is not spontaneous; it even goes against our deepest inclinations.
The first condition of debate is indeed the most improbable: to recognize that the person who contradicts us has an equal legitimacy to our own.
Nothing naturally inclines us to this.
We tend to hold our convictions as obvious, and thus explain others' disagreement by their ignorance, bad faith, or interests.
Debating requires us to suspend this reflex, to admit that the other may think differently for reasons they believe, just as we do, are good.
Without this presumption of legitimacy, there is no debate, only the confrontation of camps that mutually deny each other the right to speak.
The second condition is the existence of shared facts.
A genuine debate requires common ground, a foundation of realities that the opponents recognize together, and on which their disagreement can unfold.
Where each has their own facts, where reality itself becomes a subject of dispute, debate loses its ground: we no longer discuss interpretations of a common world, we inhabit separate worlds.
This is why the dislocation of the factual foundation — this impression that 'everyone has their truth' — is not a detail, but a threat to the very possibility of deliberation.
The third condition relates to a rare inner disposition: to accept that one could be wrong.
Anyone who enters a debate holding their conclusion as a given is not debating; they are pleading.
Authentic debate carries a risk, that of being convinced, of having to revise one's views, of leaving the exchange different from how one entered it.

This consented vulnerability is the hallmark of true debate, and its most difficult requirement, as it clashes with our attachment to our own opinions, which we experience less as hypotheses than as possessions, even as parts of ourselves.
That these conditions are so demanding explains the fragility of debate, and the ease with which it degrades into its opposite.

It is enough for just one to be lacking — for one to deny the opponent's legitimacy, for the factual foundation to dissolve, for no one to accept that they could be wrong — for deliberation to give way to invective, propaganda, and a war of camps.
Moreover, these three conditions are today simultaneously under attack, which should concern us more than the content of any particular debate.
Understanding debate as a fragile civilization, rather than as an acquired right, changes the way we view it.
This invites us to see it not as a right that merely needs to be proclaimed, but as a delicate practice that must be maintained, protected, and relearned.
A society does not suddenly stop debating overnight; it gradually loses the capacity as the conditions that made it possible unravel.
And when a people has unlearned how to debate, they are left with only paths to resolve their disagreements that history has shown to be costly.

sentences: Our time has made utility a sovereign value.

An activity, a study, an expense, even a life, is justified by what it serves; what serves no purpose is suspect, summoned to account for itself, and threatened with disappearance due to lack of profitability.

This demand for utility, which seems like simple common sense, actually exerts a discreet tyranny, as it comes to measure everything by the service it renders, and devalues everything that would be valuable in itself.
However, a civilization that no longer recognizes anything but the useful would lose what precisely gives value to existence.
First, we must see that utility is, by nature, a relative criterion: one thing is useful to another, with a view to an end that transcends it.
The hammer is useful to the nail, the nail to the board, the board to the house.
But this chain of means must stop somewhere, on something that is not useful to something else, but that is valuable in itself, and for which everything else is useful.
If everything were only useful, the chain would be endless and aimless; utility itself would have no meaning, lacking an end that is not, in turn, a mere means.
Therefore, the useful requires, to have meaning, something that escapes utility.
This something is those experiences and goods that are valuable for themselves: friendship, beauty, knowledge sought for its own sake, contemplation, play, joy.
None 'serves' any purpose in the strict sense; one does not cultivate a friendship for what it brings, nor does one contemplate a landscape for its yield.
These things are ends, not means, and it is in view of them, ultimately, that everything else is organized.

To consider them useless because they serve no other purpose is to overturn the hierarchy: it is to take means for ends, and to sacrifice what is valuable for what is only valuable for something else.
Yet it is this reversal that the tyranny of the useful enacts.
It demands that beauty justify itself by its economic utility, knowledge by its applications, leisure by its function of recovery in the service of work.
Everything must serve, and what does not serve must prove that it serves nonetheless, under threat of being abolished.
Thus, a society entirely devoted to the useful ends up no longer knowing what all this serves, having lost sight of the non-useful ends for which utility had meaning.
It produces and busies itself without knowing why, as activity has become its own justification.
This drift even affects our conception of human life.
To demand that each existence justify itself by its utility is to deny that a life can be valuable in itself, independently of what it produces or yields.
This is the slope that leads to measuring beings by their output, to considering as a burden those who no longer produce, and to recognizing dignity only in useful life.
However, a life is not a means; it is, if there is something that is valuable in itself, that very something.
Reducing existence to its utility is to miss what, in it, transcends all utility.
Defending the gratuitous against the tyranny of the useful is therefore not to advocate for idleness or waste.

It is to remind us that utility is not the supreme value, but a subordinate order, which only makes sense in service of ends that, themselves, serve no purpose because they are what everything serves.

A civilization may be judged less by what it produces than by what it knows how to preserve as gratuitous: the place it gives to beauty, to disinterested thought, to bonds that yield nothing, to all that, serving no purpose, still makes life worth living.
For what has no price, in the sense that it cannot be monetized, is also what has no price in the sense that nothing is worth it.

sentences: We live in societies that proclaim equal freedom of speech for all citizens.
Everyone, in principle, has the right to express themselves, give their opinion, and participate in the debate.
However, this principle of equality masks a more complex reality: public speech, the kind that carries weight, is not equally accessible to everyone.
It has its conditions, its guardians, and its implicit hierarchies.
Questioning who really has the right to speak — not in law, but in fact — reveals one of the deepest and least visible inequalities in our societies.
The first inequality relates to access to the means of speech.
Being able to express oneself publicly requires access to platforms, media, networks, and channels that give speech its reach.
However, these means are distributed unevenly.
Some have easy access to the public sphere due to their position, profession, or network; others, no matter what they have to say, struggle to be heard beyond their immediate circle.

Formal freedom of speech, equal for all, is thus accompanied by a real inequality in the means to make it heard, which means that the same speech does not have the same resonance depending on who utters it.
The second inequality, more subtle, relates to the legitimacy granted to the speaker.
We do not give the same attention or credit to all speeches; we rank them according to who makes them.

The words of an expert, a graduate, or a notable are listened to; those of the presumed ignorant, the subordinate, or someone who lacks the proper codes are easily disqualified, regardless of their correctness.

This hierarchy of legitimacy has its rationale — it makes sense to give more credit to those who know — but it often exceeds what would justify it, excluding voices from the debate on the grounds that they do not speak the right language, do not have the right credentials, or do not master the codes of legitimate speech.
These codes, precisely, constitute a third barrier.
Public speech follows implicit rules — a certain vocabulary, a certain tone, a certain way of arguing — mastery of which is acquired through education and environment.
Those who do not possess them are disqualified not for what they say, but for the way they say it, which is deemed clumsy, inappropriate, or illegitimate.

Thus, the very form of legitimate speech creates a social sorting, effectively reserving access to the debate for those who have acquired the codes, while excluding others under the guise of a formal requirement that masks a social exclusion.

Recognizing these inequalities does not lead to denying any hierarchy of speech, as if all were equal, as if the ignorant and the knowledgeable should be equally listened to regarding what they do not know.
There is a legitimate basis for expertise, and claiming to abolish it would lead to a populism that listens to no one because it rejects any authority of knowledge.

The problem is not that hierarchies of speech exist, but that they are unjust: that they exclude what deserves to be heard in the name of form, that they confuse the legitimacy of knowledge with the privileges of a social group, and that they silence voices for bad reasons.

The question 'who has the right to speak?' does not call for the simplistic answer 'everyone equally,' which ignores legitimate differences in competence, nor the elitist answer 'only the qualified,' which masks unjust exclusions under the guise of standards.

It calls for work: to make access to speech fairer, to listen to voices that are too quickly disqualified, to distinguish the real legitimacy of knowledge from purely social barriers, and to open the debate to those who are excluded without valid reason.
A democracy is not only measured by the freedom of speech it proclaims, but by the real equality of speech it allows — and in this regard, there is still much to be done.
