sentences: Machines now produce striking images, fluid texts, and pleasant music from just a few instructions.
This new capability disrupts our relationship with artistic creation and raises a question that is not only technical but also philosophical: is what these machines produce considered creation?
And if so, what remains unique to human creation?
This question, made urgent by current events, forces us to clarify what we mean by creating and perhaps reveals that we didn't understand it as well as we thought.
One initial reaction is to deny machines any true creation on the grounds that they merely recombine what already exists.
They have been fed countless human works, from which they extract patterns that they rearrange; they create nothing new, they recycle.
This argument is compelling, but it faces an objection: is human creation itself not largely recombination?
The human artist, too, is nourished by everything he has seen, heard, and learned; he does not create from nothing but rearranges inherited elements.
If recombination disqualifies the machine, we would also have to disqualify a part of human creation, which we refuse to do.
The boundary is therefore not so clear-cut.
A second approach seeks the difference not in the result but in the intention and experience.
The machine produces without wanting to express anything, without having lived anything, without any interiority being conveyed in what it does.
The human artist, on the other hand, creates to express something, based on an experience, a sensitivity, a relationship with the world; his work carries intention, lived experience, and presence.

What the machine would lack is not the ability to produce beautiful forms, but what, in human art, makes a work the trace of a consciousness, the expression of a being who has something to say because he has something to live.
This approach is stronger, but it shifts the difficulty rather than resolving it.

For if the value of art depends on the intention and experience of its creator, then it cannot be read in the work itself: two identical images, one made by a human expressing suffering, the other by a machine without intention, would have the same appearance but not the same value.
This means that what we value in art is not only what we perceive but also what we know about its origin.
A strange conclusion, which suggests that the value of art depends as much on its context — who made it, why, from what — as on its visible qualities.
Perhaps this is what the question of machines teaches us about art.

We discover, by asking it, that we do not value only the beautiful or the skillful, which the machine can produce, but the presence of a consciousness, the expression of lived experience, the connection with another human being.

What moves us in a work is not only its form but the fact that a being like us created it to say something; art is a communication between consciousnesses, and a production without consciousness, no matter how successful, lacks what gives it value.
The machine, by imitating the results of art, reveals to us that art was not only in its results.
This does not resolve all the practical questions raised by these machines, nor does it predict what they will become.
But it suggests that human creation retains something irreducible, not because the machine could not produce equally beautiful forms, but because what we seek in art is not just form.

In the face of machines that create, the question may not be whether they will replace artists, but rather to rediscover what we truly expected from art — and to recognize that what we expected fundamentally implied the presence of another like us, who, having lived, had something to tell us.

sentences: He made it all by himself." This phrase, spoken with admiration, celebrates someone who, starting from nothing, would have built his success solely through his own merits, without owing anything to anyone.
The myth of the self-made man, the man who makes himself, occupies a central place in the imagination of our societies, where it serves as a model and justification.
But this myth, as appealing as it may be, is based on an illusion that needs to be dispelled, as it has significant consequences for how we think about merit, success, and justice.
The illusion consists in believing that a success can be entirely the work of the person who experiences it, without owing anything to others or to circumstances.
Yet no success is ever purely individual.

The one who succeeds has benefited from countless conditions that he did not create: an education received, a language learned, knowledge accumulated by others, institutions that made his activity possible, a society that provided the framework for his success, and people who helped, trained, and supported him.
Even the most self-taught of entrepreneurs has used paths that he did not build, knowledge that he did not invent, a social order that he did not establish.
No one truly makes it all by themselves; every success is supported by a multitude of invisible contributions.
To this is added the considerable and denied part of luck.

The one who succeeds owes a lot to favorable circumstances for which he is not responsible: being born with certain talents, in a certain environment, at a certain time, meeting the right people, seizing the right opportunities, escaping the misfortunes that have shattered other trajectories.
This part of luck is completely erased by the myth of the self-made man, attributing to merit alone what owes so much to chance.

Yet for every person who has succeeded thanks to their efforts and luck, how many have made the same efforts without experiencing the same fortune, due to not having benefited from the same circumstances?
Why is this myth so tenacious, despite its obvious fragility?
Because it is flattering and reassuring, for both those who have succeeded and for the social order.

For those who have succeeded, it is gratifying to attribute their success to their own merit, rather than acknowledging what they owe to others and to luck; this justifies enjoying the full fruits of their success, without any debt to anyone.

For the social order, the myth justifies inequalities: if everyone is the architect of their own fate, then the rich deserve their wealth and the poor deserve their poverty, and the existing order is just.
The myth of the self-made man is thus an ideology that legitimizes inequalities by presenting them as the rightful reflection of merit.
Dispelling this myth has significant consequences.
Recognizing that no success is purely individual, that it owes a lot to others, to society, and to luck, is to acknowledge a debt.
The one who has succeeded does not only have rights over what he has acquired; he also has obligations to this society and to those others without whom he could not have achieved anything.
Success is not a due that one would have entirely deserved, but a shared fruit that calls for a contribution in return.
It is undermining the myth of the self-made man that allows for the foundation of the idea that those who have received the most should also give the most back.
It is not about denying all merit, pretending that efforts and qualities count for nothing, that everything is just chance and circumstances.
The one who succeeds has often, indeed, worked, persevered, and demonstrated real qualities, and it would be unjust to deny that.
It is about rejecting the opposite illusion, the one that attributes everything to the individual alone, forgetting everything that has supported him.
The truth lies in between: success combines merit, the contributions of others, and luck, and honesty consists in recognizing all three.
"I made it all by myself" is a lie, not because the one who says it has done nothing, but because he forgets everything without which what he has done would have amounted to nothing.

sentences: Democracy today enjoys such prestige that it seems almost scandalous to question it: it is regarded as the best regime, the ultimate horizon of any legitimate political organization.
However, this obviousness is recent, and the most famous praise for it is strangely paradoxical: democracy is said to be the worst of regimes, except for all the others.
This formula, half-fig, half-raisin, deserves to be taken seriously, as it expresses something true about the nature of a regime that we often celebrate without fully understanding.
Let’s start with the criticisms that democracy has always faced, and which are not without merit.

It is criticized for entrusting power to the many, that is, to a majority that is not necessarily the most competent or the wisest; for making decisions dependent on public opinion, which is fickle and manipulable; for favoring demagoguery, where the people are flattered rather than served; for prioritizing the short term, since leaders depend on upcoming elections.
These criticisms, articulated since antiquity, are not absurd: democracy indeed has these weaknesses, and claiming otherwise would be blind.
The government of the many is not the government of the best, and it can make serious mistakes.
So why prefer democracy despite everything?
The answer does not lie in the fact that it would guarantee the best decisions — it does not guarantee that — but in other virtues that compensate for its weaknesses.
The first is that it allows for a change of leaders without violence.
In non-democratic regimes, getting rid of a bad leader often requires revolt or a coup, with their accompanying violence; democracy offers a peaceful way to dismiss those who govern poorly.
This ability to correct its mistakes without bloodshed is an immense virtue, which is underestimated as long as we enjoy it.
The second virtue is that democracy, by involving the governed in decisions, recognizes a dignity that other regimes deny them.
In a democracy, the citizen is not a mere subject who obeys, but a participant, whose voice matters, who has a share in the power that governs them.
This participation, however imperfect, acknowledges each person as capable of judging, deciding, and governing themselves, rather than as a minor who needs direction.
Democracy is based on a bet on the ability of ordinary people to govern themselves — a risky bet, but one that treats them as adults rather than children.
The third virtue, linked to the previous ones, is that democracy allows for dissent, criticism, debate, and thus the correction of its own mistakes.
A regime that forbids criticism locks itself into its faults, as no one can point them out; democracy, by allowing opposition and debate, gives itself the means to recognize and correct its mistakes.
It is not infallible, but it is correctable, which is better than a claimed infallibility that prohibits any questioning.
Its strength lies not in not making mistakes, but in being able to correct itself.
The paradoxical praise of democracy then makes sense.
It is not the best regime in the sense that it would guarantee the wisest decisions; in this regard, it has real weaknesses.
But it is the best in the sense that it offers what no other does: peaceful change, the dignity of the citizen, the ability to correct itself.

These virtues do not stem from its perfection, but from its very modesty: democracy is the regime that does not claim to possess truth or wisdom, and which, knowing it can make mistakes, gives itself the means to rectify.
That is why it must be defended not as a perfect regime, but as the least bad — which, in political matters where perfection does not exist, is the highest praise one can give.
There is an intellectual temperament difference between France and Great Britain that surfaces in a thousand areas, from philosophy to politics: the relationship to the universal and the particular.

French thought tends to lean towards the universal, the grand principles, the general ideas from which consequences are drawn; British thought is wary of systems and abstractions, preferring the particular case, concrete experience, and practical solutions.
This difference, which may seem abstract, actually shapes two ways of thinking and acting in the world, and examining it sheds light on both cultures.
The French temperament is characterized by its taste for universal principles.
When faced with a question, the French mind willingly seeks the general principle it relates to, the universal rule that should apply, the idea from which one can deduce the course of action to take.
This disposition has produced declarations of principles with universal aspirations, a tradition of systematic thought, and a politics that likes to claim abstract values valid for all humanity.
It reflects a confidence in reason, in its ability to grasp universal truths and deduce the right action from them.
To think, in this tradition, is to rise to the general, to extract the principle, and to refuse to limit oneself to the particular case.
The British temperament is precisely wary of this approach.
It considers grand abstract principles suspicious, prefers experience to theory, the concrete case to the general rule, and practical solutions that work to deductions based on principles.

When faced with a question, the British mind seeks less the universal principle than the answer suited to the particular circumstances, even if it is theoretically inconsistent as long as it is effective in practice.
This disposition has produced an empiricist tradition in philosophy, a law based on precedents rather than codes, and a pragmatic politics that is distrustful of systems and proceeds by adjustments.
To think, in this tradition, is to guard against abstractions and to stay as close to experience as possible.
These two temperaments each have their strengths and dangers.

The strength of universalist thought is to rise above particularities, to establish principles valid for all, and to base action on values that transcend circumstances; its danger is to get lost in abstraction, to impose principles without regard for realities, and to sacrifice the concrete case to the logic of the system.

The strength of pragmatic thought is to remain in touch with reality, to adapt to circumstances, and to avoid the excesses of logic taken to extremes; its danger is to lack principles, to sink into opportunism, and to be unable to judge by what standard.
One risks ideology, the other the lack of a compass.
These differences manifest even in the way rights and justice are conceived.

Where the French tradition proclaims universal human rights, valid for every human being by virtue of their humanity alone, the British tradition rather claims concrete freedoms, historically acquired, rooted in customs and precedents.
One bases rights on a universal principle; the other on a particular tradition.
These two approaches can lead to similar protections, but they are founded in very different ways: one on the abstraction of a principle, the other on the concreteness of a heritage.
Understanding this difference means grasping that the universal and the particular are not just philosophical categories, but temperaments that shape entire cultures.

And it is to recognize that each needs the other: the universal without a sense of the particular becomes a dangerous abstraction, blind to realities; the particular without a sense of the universal becomes a pragmatism without principles, incapable of judgment.
Wisdom would be to hold both, to base action on principles while adapting them to circumstances, and to sacrifice neither the principle to expediency nor the real to logic.
Each tradition, by observing the other, can learn what it lacks: the French, the sense of the concrete and distrust of systems; the British, the need for principles that underpin judgment.
Their contrast is not a dispute to settle, but a complementarity to understand.

sentences: Our time has made happiness an imperative.
Not only do we want to be happy — which has always been the case — but we have turned it into a duty, a norm, an explicit and ongoing quest.
An entire industry is dedicated to making us happy; methods, advice, and techniques promise happiness; we are somehow urged to be happy, and unhappiness is considered an anomaly to be corrected.
Yet this cult of happiness, this quest elevated to an imperative, could paradoxically make us more unhappy.
We need to examine this paradox, as it touches on our very way of conceiving a successful life.
The first perverse effect of the happiness imperative is to transform ordinary unhappiness into failure.
If happiness is a duty, a norm, then not being happy becomes a fault, a shortcoming, proof that we have missed something.
Moments of sadness, doubt, and pain, which are part of every existence, stop being experienced as natural and are instead felt as failures, sources of guilt.
To suffering is added the suffering of suffering, the feeling of not measuring up to a happiness standard that we believe is universal.
The happiness imperative makes unhappiness heavier by stripping it of its legitimacy, turning it into a personal fault.
The second perverse effect relates to the very nature of the quest for happiness.
Happiness, as we have seen, eludes those who pursue it directly; it comes as a bonus when we are absorbed in something else, not when we hunt for it.
However, the happiness imperative precisely invites us to pursue it directly, to take it as a goal, to monitor it, to constantly ask ourselves if we are happy.

This anxious monitoring of one's own happiness is the best way to make it flee: by constantly watching for happiness, we cultivate dissatisfaction, we discover everything that is lacking, we spoil the happiness we seek through this surveillance.
The explicit quest for happiness, by taking it as an object, distances it.
The third perverse effect concerns comparison.
The happiness imperative is accompanied by a constant display of others' happiness: we are surrounded by images of happy lives, of displayed happiness, to which we compare our ordinary existence.
This comparison deepens dissatisfaction: our life, measured against these idealized happinesses, seems dull, insufficient, below what it should be.
We believe we are alone in not achieving the happiness that everyone else seems to know, while this displayed happiness is largely a staged performance.
The happiness imperative, by making us compare our reality to the exhibited happiness of others, feeds the feeling of our own inadequacy.
This diagnosis does not lead to renouncing happiness, nor to praising unhappiness.
It invites a change in our relationship with happiness, to free it from the imperative that distorts it.

This first requires accepting unhappiness as a normal part of existence, not as a failure: recognizing that pain, doubt, and sadness are part of every life, and that there is no fault in not being happy all the time.
It also requires stopping the direct pursuit of happiness, monitoring it, making it an anxious goal, and instead turning towards what gives meaning and joy, allowing happiness to come as a bonus.
Finally, it requires challenging displayed happiness, stopping the comparison of our reality to staged performances, and renouncing the idea that we should be as happy as we are shown to be.
The paradox of happiness is thus that its explicit quest, elevated to an imperative, turns against it.
Not that happiness is not desirable — it is — but because it cannot be grasped head-on, it cannot bear being a duty, it flees those who hunt it and gives itself to those who forget it.
Wisdom regarding happiness may not be to pursue it, but to make one's life worthy of being lived and to welcome happiness when it comes, without making it an obligation or a measure.
A life that demands to be happy at all costs is doomed not to be; a life that seeks meaning, connections, and fulfillment, and allows happiness to come as a bonus, is more likely to encounter it.
Happiness is not a goal to be achieved, but a gift to be welcomed — and trying to force it is to miss it.

sentences: We arrived in the city at noon.
The hotel was a ten-minute walk from the train station, so we walked.
The hotel was exactly like in the pictures: an old building with a blue door and flowers in the windows.
At the reception, a young woman welcomed us.
Hello!
Do you have a reservation?
Yes, under the name Martin, for two nights.
She checked on her computer.
That's perfect.
But the room isn't ready yet.
Check-in is at three o'clock.
It was a quarter past noon.
We had to wait almost three hours!
But she offered a solution.
You can leave your bags here.
We agreed and left our luggage behind the counter.
Then I asked her for advice: Where can we have lunch that isn't too expensive?
She smiled and took a map of the city.
Don't eat in the main square, it's for tourists and it's expensive.
Instead, go here, she said, pointing to a small street.
It's a family restaurant.
The lunch menu costs sixteen euros.
We followed her advice.
The restaurant was small, full of locals, and the meal was excellent.
At three o'clock, our room was ready.
It overlooked the river.
The best guide is often someone who lives there.

sentences: People often confuse the tragic with misfortune, as if everything painful, disastrous, or catastrophic were tragic.
This confusion diminishes a concept that refers to something much more precise and much deeper.

The tragic, in the strong sense, does not arise from misfortune that strikes from outside, from accidents or disasters, but from a particular structure of conflict: one in which two equally legitimate demands oppose each other without either being able to yield without fault, where duty stands against duty, and where whatever choice one makes, one is guilty.
Understanding the tragic in this way is to discover a dimension of existence that simple misfortune cannot exhaust.
The great ancient tragedies provide us with a model of this.

What is tragic there is not only that the heroes suffer and die; it is that they are caught in conflicts where every outcome is guilty, where honoring one sacred demand amounts to betraying another equally sacred.

The heroine who must choose between the laws of the city and her duties to her own, between obedience to power and loyalty to blood, does not face a simple misfortune: she faces a situation where good opposes good, where whatever choice she makes, she will fail a real duty.
There lies the tragic: not in the suffering endured, but in this tearing apart where fault is inevitable, where one can only be faithful to one value by betraying another.

This tragic structure illuminates a truth that our solution-driven era tends to obscure: not all conflicts of values can be resolved, not all legitimate demands can be reconciled, and there are situations where one cannot do good without also doing harm.
We like to believe that for every dilemma there is a good answer, that a sufficiently careful examination would allow us to decide without remainder, to do good without fault.
The tragic contradicts this reassuring belief.
It asserts that certain values are irreducibly in conflict, that one cannot honor them all, and that the choice, therefore, is a tearing apart rather than a solution.
Recognizing the tragic is to renounce the illusion that every moral dilemma has an innocent outcome.
This recognition has a significance that goes beyond the tragic scene.

For life itself contains its share of the tragic, those situations where we are caught between irreconcilable duties, where we must betray one attachment to honor another, sacrifice one value to save another.

The parent who must choose between their duties to their children and those to their elderly parents; the one who must betray a friend to be faithful to justice; the one who can save one only by abandoning the other: these experience the tragic, this tearing apart where one cannot do good without also doing harm.

Life is not only made up of choices between good and evil, where the difficulty lies in wanting good; it is also made up of choices between good and good, where whatever side one takes, one fails at something.
What to do with this recognition of the tragic?
It does not lead to despair or paralysis, as if the inevitability of fault should discourage any action.
Rather, it leads to a form of lucidity and gravity.
Lucidity: not to deceive oneself about the nature of certain choices, not to pretend they are innocent when they are not, to recognize what one sacrifices in choosing.
Gravity: to measure the weight of these choices, to assume the share of fault, not to give oneself a clear conscience at little cost.

The tragic teaches us to act while recognizing that our action, in certain situations, carries an inevitable share of harm, and to bear this share without falsely absolving ourselves or burdening ourselves fruitlessly.

The tragic is therefore not misfortune, but a truth about the structure of moral existence: that there are conflicts of values that cannot be resolved, situations where duty opposes duty, where fault is inevitable.
Recognizing this is to gain a deeper wisdom than that which believes in the harmony of all values and the innocence of all good choices.

It is to understand that living as a moral being is not only to want good against evil, but also to confront, sometimes, the tearing apart where good opposes good — and to assume, with lucidity and gravity, the share of fault that then accompanies every choice.
This recognition of the tragic, far from being pessimism, may be the mark of a moral consciousness that has reached its full maturity.

sentences: It is a singular experience, distinct from that of beauty, which thinkers have named the sublime.

In the face of certain realities that surpass us — the immensity of the sea or the starry sky, the unleashed power of a storm, the dizzying height of mountains — we experience something complex and paradoxical: a mix of fear and exhilaration, a feeling of our smallness and elevation, an emotion where the displeasure of feeling crushed transforms into a strange pleasure.
This experience of the sublime, different from the gentle satisfaction provided by beauty, deserves to be analyzed, as it reveals something profound about our condition and the resources of our mind.
What distinguishes the sublime from beauty is primarily its object and the feeling it evokes.
Beauty pleases us through its harmonious, proportionate form, which aligns with our sensitivity; it calms us, satisfies us, charms us.
The sublime, on the other hand, arises from what exceeds all form, all measure, all proportion: the immense, the formless, the disproportionate, that which surpasses our ability to grasp and measure.
And the feeling it evokes is not the gentle satisfaction of beauty, but a violent, mixed emotion, where the fear of what crushes us combines with exhilaration.
The sublime does not charm; it seizes, it disturbs, it elevates even in turmoil.
How can we explain this paradox of pleasure born from what crushes us?
Thinkers have proposed a subtle analysis.

In the face of the immense, the powerful, the disproportionate, we first experience our own smallness, our powerlessness, the limits of our capacity to grasp: this is the moment of fear, of displeasure.

But in that very movement, something within us reveals itself that surpasses this smallness: our capacity to think the infinite that we cannot perceive, to conceive what exceeds our senses, to elevate ourselves by the mind above what physically crushes us.
The sublime makes us experience our sensitive smallness, but also, by contrast, the greatness of our mind, capable of thinking what surpasses it.
The pleasure of the sublime arises from this discovery: that, while we are small in the face of immensity, we carry within us something that is not measured by it, a dimension that surpasses it.
This analysis has implications that go beyond aesthetics.

For the sublime reveals a truth about our condition: that we are beings both tiny and immense, crushed by the disproportion of the world yet capable of thinking it, conceiving it, measuring ourselves against it by the mind.
We are reeds, said a thinker, the weakest of nature, easily crushed by a trifle; but we are thinking reeds, and through thought, we embrace the universe that crushes us.
The sublime is the aesthetic experience of this dual condition: it makes us feel our smallness and, in the same movement, the greatness of what, within us, surpasses this smallness.
It is like a sensitive revelation of the paradoxical dignity of man.
The experience of the sublime also holds value in a world that tends to forget it.
For we are increasingly living in a humanized, controlled environment, tailored to our measure, from which the disproportionate, the immense, that which surpasses us, tends to disappear.
Our cities, our screens, our confined existences shield us from encountering what exceeds the human.
Yet this encounter has value: it displaces us, reminds us of our smallness, tears us away from the disproportion of our own importance.
The sublime is a lesson in humility, but a humility that does not belittle; on the contrary, it elevates us by placing us in the presence of what surpasses us.

A civilization that has lost all experience of the sublime, all contact with what exceeds it, would be a shriveled civilization, confined within its own measure, deprived of the elevation that the encounter with the immense provides.

Cultivating the experience of the sublime, arranging for encounters with what surpasses us — nature in its disproportion, the immensity of the sky, the power of the elements, but also the greatness of certain works, thoughts, and actions — is therefore essential to preserving a vital dimension of our humanity.
The sublime reminds us that we are not the measure of all things, that something surpasses us, and that in this very encounter, what we hold highest is revealed.

In a world that confines us to our own measure, that reduces everything to the human, the useful, the manageable, the experience of the sublime is like an open window onto the immense, a reminder of our intertwined smallness and greatness.
It may be one of the experiences that humanity needs most, and from which our time deprives us the most.

sentences: This winter, it hasn't snowed a single time here.
Not once.
In December, in January, in February: it was gray and damp, with temperatures of eight or ten degrees.
It rained a lot, but the water remained just water.
My children were disappointed.
My daughter asked me, "Are we going to make a snowman this year?" I replied, "We'll see." We didn't make one.
This isn't the first time.
Last winter, it snowed only one day, and the snow melted before evening.
One Sunday, we had lunch at my grandmother's.
My daughter talked to her about the snow.
My grandmother smiled, then she told stories about her childhood in the same village.
Every winter, there was snow for weeks.
My brother and I would go to school on skis because the road was closed.
My daughter looked at her with wide eyes.
Skis?
To go to school?
Every winter,” replied my grandmother.
Then she added, “Here, snow was normal.
Now, it's an event.”
In the car, my daughter was silent.
Then she asked, “Will it still snow when I am grown up?”
I didn't know what to say.

sentences: Forgiveness is regarded as a great virtue, a transcendence of vengeance, a liberation for both the one who grants it and the one who receives it.
But as soon as we reflect on it, forgiveness reveals itself to be filled with formidable paradoxes.
Are there unforgivable offenses, or can everything be forgiven?
Does forgiveness have meaning if it is always owed, or does it precisely imply that it could be refused?
Must the guilty party repent in order to be forgiven, or can forgiveness be unconditional?
These questions, far from being trivial, touch on what is most profound and most difficult about forgiveness.
Let's first consider the question of unforgivable wrongs.
One position holds that everything can be forgiven, that there is no wrong that forgiveness cannot reach, and that refusing to forgive would be a failure of virtue.
This position has its grandeur: it asserts the unlimited power of forgiveness, its ability to overcome the worst.
But it faces a formidable objection: some wrongs seem so egregious that forgiving them would trivialize them, betray the victims, and erase the horror.
Can we, should we forgive extreme crimes, those that go beyond all measure?
And who could do it?
Certainly not third parties, who have not suffered the wrong; and the victims themselves, when they are no longer there to forgive, leave the wrong in a kind of irredeemable state.
It seems that there are wrongs that exceed forgiveness, not because forgiveness is limited, but because forgiving them would be an injustice to what they have destroyed.
Here we encounter a first paradox: forgiveness may only make sense in the face of what seems unforgivable.
For forgiving what is easily excusable, a minor fault, a trivial offense, is not really forgiveness; it is excusing, forgetting, letting it go.
Forgiveness in the strong sense only begins where excuses are no longer sufficient, in the face of a real, serious fault that could legitimately provoke resentment.
Forgiveness presupposes the fault, a fault that cannot be excused, and it precisely consists of not demanding the punishment that this fault would deserve, renouncing legitimate resentment.
Thus, true forgiveness is only exercised in the face of what, in a sense, does not deserve it; it is gratuitous, exceeding what is owed.
If it were always owed, it would no longer be forgiveness, but justice; it is because it could be refused that it has the value of a gift.
A second paradox concerns the condition of forgiveness.
Must the guilty party repent, acknowledge their fault, and ask for forgiveness in order to be forgiven?
This condition seems reasonable: how can one forgive someone who regrets nothing, persists in their wrongdoing, and does not ask for forgiveness?
Forgiveness granted to someone who does not repent seems futile, even complicit.
And yet, subordinating forgiveness to repentance may distort it: for then forgiveness becomes conditional, deserved, almost owed to the one who repents, and it loses its gratuitousness.
The highest, most difficult form of forgiveness might be the one granted unconditionally, without waiting for repentance, as a pure grace.
But does such unconditional forgiveness not risk trivializing the wrongdoing, freeing the guilty party from any self-reflection?
The paradox lies here: conditional forgiveness may not be true forgiveness, but unconditional forgiveness risks injustice.
These paradoxes do not have simple solutions, and it would be presumptuous to claim to resolve them.

But they reveal the profound nature of forgiveness: that it is neither a right nor an oblivion, neither justice nor complacency, but something excessive, gratuitous, and almost impossible, which only makes sense in the face of what seems to reject it.
True forgiveness is difficult precisely because it is not owed, because it is exercised in the face of what could legitimately provoke resentment, because it exceeds justice without abolishing it.

It consists neither in excusing the wrongdoing, nor in forgetting it, nor in renouncing justice, but in overcoming personal resentment, in not allowing the wrongdoing to poison indefinitely the one who has suffered it.
What remains, in light of these paradoxes, is that forgiveness, if it is possible, is a liberation, but a liberation primarily for the one who forgives.
For resentment, hatred, and the desire for revenge first poison the one who harbors them; forgiveness, by renouncing them, frees the one who grants it from the poison of their own bitterness.

Forgiveness does not erase the fault, does not bring justice, does not resurrect what has been destroyed; but it liberates the one who forgives from the grip of the wrong suffered, refusing to let the harm received continue to dominate them through resentment.
In this sense, even in the face of what seems unforgivable, a form of forgiveness can be a victory: not over the fault, which remains, but over its power to confine us in hatred.

To forgive may not be to absolve the guilty, but to free oneself — and perhaps it is in this liberation that the deepest and most accessible meaning of forgiveness lies, one that can never be an acquittal regarding certain wrongs.

sentences: A civilization does not sustain itself; it only survives by transmitting what it holds most precious from one generation to the next — its knowledge, its values, its works, its ways of life.
Transmission is thus the vital act through which a civilization perpetuates itself, recreates itself in each generation, and escapes death.
However, this transmission, which was once almost naturally assured, has become difficult, uncertain, and threatened.
And this difficulty in transmitting is not a minor issue; it touches on the very survival of what we hold most precious, on the continuity of civilization itself.
What does it mean to transmit?
It is not just about communicating information or teaching techniques; it is about passing on a living heritage, a world of meaning, values, works, and ways of being from one generation to another.
Transmitting means giving to those who come after us what we have received from those who preceded us, placing them in a continuity, bequeathing them a world that they will make their own in turn.
It is an act of fidelity to the past and responsibility to the future, the link that connects generations in a continuous chain.
Without transmission, each generation would have to reinvent everything, start from scratch; it is through transmission that humanity accumulates, perpetuates itself, and does not keep starting over.
However, this transmission is currently made difficult by several factors.
The pace of change, first: in a world that is transforming so quickly, the legacy of past generations seems quickly outdated, surpassed, and worthless for a present that has broken away from it.
Why pass on what seems obsolete?

The rift between generations, next: the gap that separates them, the impression that young people live in a world so different that the experiences of the elders no longer concern them, makes transmission more challenging.

The devaluation of the past, finally: a culture focused on novelty, the present, and the future tends to despise heritage, to regard it as a burden rather than a treasure, and to value rupture over continuity.
This difficulty in transmitting has serious consequences that are poorly understood.

For what is not transmitted is lost; and a civilization that ceases to transmit itself would unravel, not through a sudden catastrophe, but through the silent erosion of what would no longer be bequeathed.

The accumulated knowledge, the works, the values, the ways of being that constitute a civilization survive only when transmitted; if we stop transmitting them, they fade away, not because they have been destroyed, but because they have not been passed on.
The breakdown of transmission is not just another educational issue; it poses a threat to the very continuity of civilization, an oblivion that erases what centuries have accumulated.
What is needed for transmission to be possible?

First, those who transmit must have something to pass on that they consider valuable, and they must want to transmit it; a generation that despises its own heritage, that sees nothing in it worth bequeathing, would transmit nothing.
Next, those who receive must be willing to accept, not rejecting by principle the heritage of past generations, and they must recognize that they have something to receive.

Finally, there must be places, institutions, and relationships where transmission can take place: schools, families, teachers, all those places where heritage is passed from one generation to another.
Transmission relies on a chain of goodwill, fidelity, and recognition, without which it breaks.
Caring for transmission is therefore one of the most essential and most neglected responsibilities of our time.

For we have inherited a world that we did not create, built and passed down by generations before us; and we have the responsibility to transmit it in turn, not to break the chain, not to squander a heritage that we only hold temporarily.
Transmitting what we hold most precious — knowledge, works, values, memory — ensures the survival of civilization, connecting it to its past and future, refusing to let it unravel into oblivion.

In a world that values rupture and despises heritage, rehabilitating transmission, taking care of it, wanting it, is perhaps one of the most urgent tasks for those who care about not losing civilization.
For a civilization does not only die from its catastrophes; it also dies, more silently, from ceasing to transmit itself.

sentences: Since the dawn of humanity, people have sought to conquer death, to achieve a form of immortality.

This quest has taken a thousand forms: belief in an afterlife, the pursuit of enduring glory, the desire to leave a lasting legacy, the passing on to descendants, and today, dreams of a science that would abolish death.
This stubbornness to want to conquer death, across ages and cultures, reveals something profound about our condition and about who we are.
What does this quest for immortality teach us about ourselves?
It first reveals the depth of our refusal of death, our desire to live, our revolt against finitude.
Humans are the only beings who know they will die, and this knowledge generates a refusal, a revolt, a quest to escape what burdens us.
This quest for immortality is the expression of our deepest desire: not to die, not to cease to be, to escape annihilation.
It testifies to humanity's attachment to life, its refusal of finitude, its revolt against the mortal condition.
In seeking immortality, humans express what is most fundamental to them: the desire to be, against the threat of non-being.
It also reveals the need for meaning, for permanence, for what lasts beyond the ephemeral.
For man is not content to exist in the moment; he aspires to what endures, to what escapes the flow of time, to a permanence that gives meaning to the ephemeral.
The quest for immortality is also a quest for meaning, for permanence, for what withstands the passage of time that takes everything away.

In the face of universal flight, of the impermanence of all things, man seeks what lasts, what endures, what escapes annihilation; and this quest expresses his need for meaning, his refusal of the insignificance of what passes without leaving a trace.
But this quest may also reveal an illusion, or at least an ambivalence.
For we have seen that immortality, if it were to be realized, could abolish what gives life its value — the finitude that makes time precious, the decisive choices, the intensity of what passes.
The quest for immortality, while it expresses a deep desire, could aim at something that, if realized, would disappoint, by taking away from life what makes it precious.
There is an ambivalence in this quest: we desire immortality, and yet immortality might not be the good we believe it to be, it could abolish the very meaning we seek.
Perhaps what we are really seeking is not to never die, but to give our mortal life a meaning that transcends it.
For there are forms of immortality that are not the abolition of death, but the transcendence of its finitude through meaning.

Leaving behind a work, a mark, an influence that survives; contributing to something larger and more enduring than oneself; being part of a continuity that exceeds our individual existence: these are forms of transcending death that do not abolish it, but give our mortal life a significance that surpasses its duration.

This kind of immortality — not biological, but through meaning, work, mark, contribution — may be what we are truly seeking, one that answers our need for meaning and permanence without abolishing what gives value to finite life.
Not to never die, but for our passage to have a meaning that transcends it.
Thus, the quest for immortality, if understood correctly, may not aim so much at the abolition of death as at the transcendence of its finitude through meaning.

What we are really seeking may not be to never die — which would abolish the value of life — but to give our mortal life a meaning that transcends it, a significance that exceeds our duration, a mark that survives.
This kind of immortality is within our reach, not through science or a miracle, but through the way we live, through what we leave behind, through the meaning we give to our passage.
We will not conquer death; but we can make our mortal life have a meaning that transcends it, a value that survives, a mark that remains.

And perhaps this is the only immortality accessible to us, and the only one worth having: not the impossible and perhaps undesirable abolition of death, but the meaning we imbue our finite life with — this way of living that ensures that an existence, though mortal, will not have passed in vain.

sentences: Once the first page was turned, she let me browse through it at my leisure; and I flipped through so many chapters that our candles burned down completely.

Then, after thanking her, I was making my way back to my room quietly when a rough hand stopped me; and a voice, that of Rivet, whispered in my ear: "Haven't you finished sorting out that pig of Morin's yet?" From seven in the morning, she herself brought me a cup of chocolate.
I've never had any like it.
A chocolate to die for, rich, velvety, fragrant, intoxicating.
I couldn't take my mouth away from the delicious rim of her cup.
Hardly had the young girl left when Rivet entered.

He seemed a bit nervous, irritated like a man who hasn't slept much; he said to me in a grumpy tone: "If you keep this up, you know, you'll end up ruining that pig of Morin's business." At eight o'clock, my aunt arrived.
The discussion was brief.
The good people withdrew their complaint, and I would leave five hundred francs to the poor of the area.
Then they wanted to keep us to spend the day.
They would even organize an outing to visit some ruins.
Henriette, behind her parents' backs, was nodding at me: "Yes, do stay." I accepted, but Rivet was determined to leave.

sentences: From then on, she drank vinegar to lose weight, developed a slight dry cough, and completely lost her appetite.
It was hard for Charles to leave Tostes after four years of living there, especially when he was just starting to settle in.
If necessary, however!
He took her to Rouen to see her former teacher.
It was a nervous illness: she needed a change of air.
After turning this way and that, Charles learned that there was a large town called Yonville-l’Abbaye in the Neufchâtel district, where the doctor, a Polish refugee, had just fled the previous week.

So he wrote to the local pharmacist to find out the population number, the distance to the nearest colleague, how much his predecessor earned per year, etc.; and, having received satisfactory answers, he decided to move in the spring if Emma's health did not improve.
One day, while preparing for her departure and tidying up a drawer, she pricked her fingers on something.
It was a wire from her wedding bouquet.
The orange blossoms were yellow with dust, and the satin ribbons, edged with silver, were fraying at the edges.
She threw it into the fire.
It ignited faster than dry straw.
Then it was like a red bush on the ashes, slowly consuming itself.
She watched it burn.
The little cardboard berries burst, the wires twisted, the trim melted; and the crumpled paper corollas, swaying along the plate like black butterflies, finally flew up the chimney.

sentences: At the Barrière du Trône, they encountered Bertuccio: he was waiting there, motionless like a sentinel at his post.
Monte-Cristo leaned his head out of the window, exchanged a few quiet words with him, and the steward disappeared.
"Count, said Emmanuel as he reached the Place Royale, please have me dropped off at my door, so that my wife won't have a moment's worry about either you or me.

--Just a moment, said Monte-Cristo, don't deprive me of both my companions at once; go back to your lovely wife, to whom I charge you to send my best regards, and accompany me to the Champs-Élysées, Morrel.
--Wonderful, said Maximilien, especially since I have business in your area, Count.
"See how I've brought you good luck, said Morrel when he was alone with the count.
Haven't you thought of that?
--Indeed, said Monte-Cristo, that's why I always want to keep you close to me.
--Yes, replied the count with a smile; you hit the nail on the head, Morrel, it's miraculous!
--Very brave, said Monte-Cristo, I saw him sleeping with the dagger hanging over his head.
--And I know that he fought twice, and fought very well, said Morrel; so reconcile that with his behavior this morning.

And everyone formed a circle around the fire again, while Diavolaccio moved away.
The bandits looked at him in astonishment, not understanding this impassivity, when they heard a heavy step behind them echoing on the ground.
They turned around and saw Diavolaccio holding the young girl in his arms.
Her head was thrown back, and her long hair hung down to the ground.
As they entered the circle of light cast by the fire, one could see the paleness of the young girl and the paleness of the bandit.
This appearance was so strange and so solemn that everyone stood up, except for Carlini, who remained seated and continued to eat and drink as if nothing was happening around him.
Diavolaccio continued to advance in the deepest silence and laid Rita at the captain's feet.
Then everyone could recognize the cause of the young girl's paleness and the bandit's paleness: Rita had a knife plunged to the hilt beneath her left breast.
All eyes turned to Carlini: the sheath was empty at his belt.
Ah!
Ah!
said the chief, I now understand why Carlini stayed behind.
Any wild nature is capable of appreciating a strong action; although perhaps none of the bandits would have done what Carlini just did, they all understood what he had done.

sentences: These thoughts came back to me as I considered the coal riches accumulated in this part of the earth's massif.
These, no doubt, will never be uncovered.
The exploitation of these remote mines would require too considerable sacrifices.
What's the point, anyway, when coal is practically spread across the surface of the earth in many regions?
Thus, as I saw these untouched layers, so they would remain even when the world's last hour strikes.
However, we were walking, and only among my companions did I forget the length of the road to lose myself in geological considerations.
The temperature remained roughly what it was during our passage through the lavas and schists.
Only, my sense of smell was affected by a very strong odor of hydrogen proto-carbide.
I immediately recognized, in this gallery, the presence of a significant quantity of this dangerous gas that miners call firedamp, which has often caused terrible disasters.
Fortunately, we were illuminated by the ingenious devices of Ruhmkorff.
If, unfortunately, we had carelessly explored this gallery with a torch in hand, a terrible explosion would have ended the journey by eliminating the travelers.
This excursion into the coal mine lasted until evening.
My uncle could barely contain the impatience caused by the horizontal nature of the road.

The darkness, always deep twenty paces ahead, made it impossible to gauge the length of the gallery, and I began to believe it was endless when suddenly, at six o'clock, a wall unexpectedly appeared before us.
To the right, to the left, above, below, there was no passage.
We had reached the end of a dead end.

sentences: I took her hand, a bit confused, stammering: "Sorry, sorry, miss.
I hurt you; I was brutal!
Don't hold it against me.
If you only knew?..." I was vainly searching for an excuse.
After a moment, she said: "I have nothing to know, sir." But I had found it; I exclaimed: "Miss, I've loved you for a year!" She was truly surprised and looked up.
I continued: "Yes, miss, listen to me.
I don't know Morin and I don't care about him.
I couldn't care less if he goes to prison and faces the courts.
I saw you here last year, you were over there, by the gate.
I felt a jolt when I saw you and your image has never left me.
Believe me, or don't believe me, I couldn't care less.
I found you adorable; your memory possessed me; I wanted to see you again; I seized the pretext of that stupid Morin; and here I am.

Circumstances pushed me beyond my limits; forgive me, I beg you, forgive me." She was watching for the truth in my eyes, ready to smile again; and she murmured: "Joker." I raised my hand, and, in a sincere tone (I even believe I was sincere): "I swear to you I'm not lying." We were alone, completely alone, Rivet and the uncle having disappeared into the winding paths; and I made a real declaration to her, long, sweet, pressing and kissing her fingers.
She listened to this as something pleasant and new, not quite knowing what to believe about it.
I ended up feeling troubled; thinking about what I was saying; I was pale, oppressed, shivering; and gently, I took her waist.

Morrel gave a smile that closely resembled a grimace and turned to Monte-Cristo, as if asking him to help him out of the embarrassment he was in.

madame, he replied, "why is it that this request is not directed at me?"

It's pine, fir, birch, all the species of conifers from the North, mineralized under the action of seawater.

Mrs. Lefèvre was a country lady, a widow, one of those half-peasant women with ribbons and frilly hats, one of those people who speak with airs of grandeur, put on a show in public, and hide a pretentious brutish soul beneath comical and colorful exteriors, just as they conceal their large red hands under raw silk gloves.
The two women lived in a small house with green shutters, along a road in Normandy, in the heart of the Pays de Caux.
Since they had a narrow garden in front of the house, they grew some vegetables.
As soon as Rose noticed the theft, she ran to inform her mistress, who came down wearing a wool skirt.
It was a desolation and a terror.
They had stolen, stolen Mrs. Lefèvre!
So, theft was happening in the area, and they could come back.
And the two frightened women gazed at the footprints, chatted, and speculated: 'Look, they passed through here.
They put their feet on the wall; they jumped into the flowerbed.' The news of the theft spread.
The neighbors arrived, confirmed the situation, discussed it in turn; and the two women explained their observations and ideas to each newcomer.
A farmer from nearby offered them this advice: 'You should get a dog.' Once everyone had left, Mrs. Lefèvre pondered this idea of a dog for a long time.

After some thought, she raised a thousand objections, terrified by the image of a bowl full of dog food; for she belonged to that frugal breed of country ladies who always carry coins in their pockets to ostentatiously give alms to the poor on the roads and to contribute to Sunday collections.

sentences: However, I was returning from a difficult journey, tired and eager for rest.
I longed only to see my country, my friends, my little home in the Jardin des Plantes, and my dear and precious collections!
But nothing could hold me back.
I forgot everything—fatigue, friends, collections—and I accepted the offer from the American government without further thought.
Besides, I thought, every road leads back to Europe, and the Licorne will be kind enough to take me towards the shores of France!
This worthy creature will allow itself to be caught in the seas of Europe
--for my personal enjoyment

--and I don't want to bring back less than half a meter of its ivory halberd to the Natural History Museum." But in the meantime, I had to search for this narwhal in the northern Pacific Ocean; which, to return to France, meant taking the path to the antipodes.
Conseil was my servant.

A devoted boy who accompanied me on all my travels; a brave Fleming whom I loved and who returned my affection, a phlegmatic being by nature, regular by principle, zealous by habit, rarely surprised by life's surprises, very skillful with his hands, capable of any service, and, despite his name, never giving advice.
—even when it wasn't asked of him.
By rubbing shoulders with the scholars of our little world at the Jardin des Plantes, Conseil had come to know something.

I had in him a specialist, very knowledgeable about classification in natural history, navigating with the agility of an acrobat through the entire hierarchy of groups, classes, subclasses, orders, families, genera, subgenera, species, and varieties.
But his knowledge stopped there.
Classifying was his life, and he didn't know any more than that.
Very well-versed in the theory of classification, but lacking in practice, he wouldn't have been able to distinguish, I believe, a sperm whale from a baleen whale!
And yet, what a brave and worthy young man!

alignments.french: Le gardien, qui est en même temps fossoyeur et bedeau à l’église (tirant ainsi des cadavres de la paroisse un double bénéfice), a profité du terrain vide pour y semer des pommes de terre.
alignments.english: The caretaker, who is also the gravedigger and sexton at the church (thus drawing a double benefit from the parish corpses), has taken advantage of the empty land to plant potatoes.

alignments.french: D’année en année, cependant, son petit champ se rétrécit, et, lorsqu’il survient une épidémie, il ne sait pas s’il doit se réjouir des décès ou s’affliger des sépultures.
alignments.english: Year after year, however, his small field shrinks, and when an epidemic occurs, he doesn't know whether to rejoice at the deaths or to mourn the burials.

sentences: Such was, in summary, the important question that the precise observations of Thomas Black and Jasper Hobson were about to resolve.
At that moment, the sun was approaching the highest point of its course.
The two observers then aimed the telescope of their sextant at the star that was still rising.

By means of the inclined mirrors placed on the instrument, the sun was to be, apparently, brought back to the very horizon, and the moment when it would seem to touch it by the lower edge of its disk would be precisely the moment when it occupied the highest point of the daily arc, and therefore, the exact moment when it would pass the meridian, that is to say, noon at that location.
--Noon!" replied Thomas Black at that very moment.
The telescopes were immediately lowered.
The lieutenant and the astronomer read the values of the angles they had just obtained from the graduated limbs and immediately set to work calculating their observations.

A few minutes later, Lieutenant Hobson stood up and, addressing his companions, said to them, "My friends, from this day, July 6, the Hudson's Bay Company, committing by my word, doubles the salary that is assigned to you!
Hurrah!
Hurrah!
Hurrah for the Company!" shouted the worthy companions of Lieutenant Hobson in unison.
Indeed, Cape Bathurst and the surrounding territory were undoubtedly located above the seventieth parallel.

Here are, to within a second, the coordinates that would later have such great importance for the future of the new fort: And this very evening, these bold pioneers, camped so far from the inhabited world, over eight hundred miles from Fort Reliance, saw the radiant star skim the edges of the western horizon, without even denting its blazing disk.
The midnight sun shone for the first time in their eyes.
The location of the fort was irrevocably decided.

sentences: It was high time for Thomas Black.
Five more minutes, and the astronomer would have been frozen in place!
On December 2nd, the intensity of the cold had decreased.
These parhelion phenomena were a symptom that a meteorologist could not have mistaken.

They noted the presence of a certain amount of water vapor in the atmosphere, and indeed, the barometer dropped slightly, while the thermometer rose to fifteen degrees above zero (–90 degrees Celsius).
Although this cold still seemed harsh in any region of the temperate zone, professional winterers were handling it easily.
Moreover, the atmosphere was calm.
Lieutenant Hobson, having observed that the upper layers of icy snow had softened, ordered the clearing of the outer surroundings of the enclosure.
Mac Nap and his men undertook this task with courage, and within a few days it was successfully completed.
At the same time, they uncovered the buried traps, and they were reset.
Numerous tracks proved that fur-bearing game was gathering around the cape, and with the ground offering no food, they would easily be lured into the traps.
Following the advice of the hunter Marbre, they also built a reindeer snare, using the method of the Eskimos.
It was a pit about ten feet wide in all directions and about twelve feet deep.
A board acting as a seesaw, which could lift itself by its own weight, covered it in such a way as to completely conceal it.
The animal, attracted by the grasses and branches placed at the end of the board, was inevitably plunged into the pit, from which it could no longer escape.
It is understood that, with this seesaw system, the snare reset automatically, and that once a reindeer was caught, others could fall into it in turn.
Marbre encountered no other difficulty in setting up his snare than drilling through very hard ground; but he was quite surprised.
and Jasper Hobson was no less so
when the pickaxe, after having gone through four to five feet of earth and sand, encountered below a layer of snow, as hard as rock, which seemed to be very thick.

"It is necessary, said Lieutenant Hobson, after observing this geological arrangement, that this part of the coastline must have been subjected, many years ago, to extreme cold for a very long period; then, the sands and earth must have gradually covered the ice mass, presumably spread over a bed of granite.

sentences: Protésilas listened to all these praises with a dry, distracted, and disdainful air, like a man who knows he deserves even greater ones and who is too gracious to allow himself to be praised.
There was a flatterer who took the liberty of speaking to him in his ear to say something amusing against the authority that Mentor was trying to establish.
Protésilas smiled; the whole assembly immediately burst into laughter, although most could not yet know what had been said.
But Protésilas soon resumed his severe and haughty demeanor, and everyone fell back into fear and silence.

Several nobles were looking for the moment when Protésilas might turn to them and listen: they appeared moved and embarrassed; they had favors to ask of him; their pleading posture spoke for them; they seemed as submissive as a mother at the feet of the altars when she asks the gods for the healing of her only son.
Everyone seemed pleased, touched, filled with admiration for Protésilas, although all harbored in their hearts an unrelenting rage against him.
At that moment, Hégésippe entered, seized Protésilas's sword, and declared to him, on behalf of the king, that he was going to take him to the island of Samos.
At these words, all the arrogance of this favorite fell away, like a rock detaching from the top of a steep mountain.

There he was, trembling and troubled, throwing himself at Hégésippe's feet; he cried, hesitated, stammered, trembled; he embraced the knees of this man whom he had not deigned to honor with a glance just an hour before.
All those who had been praising him, seeing him lost and without resources, turned their flattery into merciless insults.
Hégésippe did not want to give him time to say his last goodbyes to his family or to take certain secret writings.
Everything was seized and taken to the king.
Timocrate was arrested at the same time: and his surprise was extreme; for he believed that being at odds with Protésilas, he could not be caught up in his downfall.
They departed on a ship that had been prepared.
They arrived at Samos.
Hégésippe left these two unfortunate men there; and, to add to their misfortune, he left them together.

There, they furiously reproached each other for the crimes they had committed, which were the cause of their downfall: they found themselves without hope of seeing Salente again, condemned to live far from their wives and children; I do not mention their friends, for they had none.
They were being taken to an unknown land, where they would have no other means of living than their labor, they who had spent so many years in luxury and splendor.
Like two wild beasts, they were always ready to tear each other apart.

sentences: We used to throw our caps on the ground when we entered the classroom, so that we would have our hands freer afterward; as soon as we crossed the threshold, we had to launch them under the bench, so they would hit the wall and create a lot of dust; that was the way it was.
But whether he hadn’t noticed this maneuver or hadn’t dared to comply, by the time the prayer was over, the newcomer was still holding his cap on his knees.

It was one of those composite hats, where you can find elements of a fur cap, a chapska, a round hat, an otter cap, and a cotton bonnet, one of those poor things, in short, whose silent ugliness has depths of expression like the face of a fool.

Ovoid and bulging with whalebones, it started with three circular rolls; then, separated by a red band, there alternated diamonds of velvet and rabbit fur; next came a sort of bag that ended in a cardboard polygon, covered with a complicated soutache embroidery, from which hung, at the end of a long, too-thin cord, a small cross of golden threads, like a tassel.
It was new; the visor was shining.
He stood up; his cap fell.
The whole class burst out laughing.
He bent down to pick it up.
A classmate knocked it down with an elbow, and he picked it up once again.
Remove your cap, then, said the professor, who was a witty man.
There was a loud laugh from the schoolboys that flustered the poor boy, so much so that he didn't know whether to keep his cap in his hand, leave it on the ground, or put it on his head.
He sat back down and placed it on his knees.
The same mumbling of syllables was heard, drowned out by the jeers of the class.
The newcomer, then making an extreme decision, opened his mouth wide and shouted at the top of his lungs, as if to call someone, the word: Charbovari.
It was a racket that sprang up suddenly, rising in crescendo, with sharp bursts of voices (they were yelling, barking, stamping their feet, repeating: Charbovari!

Charbovari!), then rolling into isolated notes, calming down with great difficulty, and sometimes suddenly picking up again along the line of a bench where, like a poorly extinguished firecracker, some muffled laughter still popped up here and there.

Say it!” As for the old man, his labored breathing shook his chest.
It seemed as if he were in the throes of those agitations that precede death.
Finally, tears burst forth from Noirtier's eyes, happier than the young man who sobbed without crying.
His head unable to bend, his eyes closed.
Say that she was my noble friend, my only love on earth!
And the young man, presenting the terrible sight of great strength breaking, fell heavily to his knees before the bed, which his clenched fingers gripped violently.

This pain was so piercing that d'Avrigny turned away to hide his emotion, and Villefort, without asking for further explanation, drawn by that magnetism that pulls us toward those who have loved those we mourn, extended his hand to the young man.
But Morrel saw nothing; he had grasped Valentine’s cold hand, and, unable to cry, he bit the sheets while roaring.
For a while, the only sounds heard in that room were the conflict of sobs, curses, and prayer.
And yet one sound dominated all of those, it was the hoarse and wrenching gasp that seemed, with each breath, to break one of the springs of life in Noirtier's chest.
Finally, Villefort, the most composed of all, after having, so to speak, ceded his place for a time to Maximilien, took the floor.

Sir, he said to Maximilien, you loved Valentine, you say: you were her fiancé; I was unaware of this love, I was unaware of this commitment; and yet, I, her father, forgive you, for I see that your pain is great, real, and true.

But, you see, the angel you hoped for has left this earth: she no longer cares for the adoration of men, she who, at this hour, worships the Lord; so say your goodbyes, sir, to the sad remains she has left among us; take her hand one last time, and part from her forever: Valentine no longer needs anything but the priest who is to bless her.

sentences: He found it lamentable to live in this village, with Homais as a friend and Mr.
Guillaumin as a master.

The latter, completely absorbed in business, wearing gold-rimmed glasses and sporting a red beard on a white cravat, understood nothing of the subtleties of the mind, although he affected a stiff and English manner that had dazzled the clerk in the early days.

As for the pharmacist's wife, she was the best wife in Normandy, gentle as a lamb, cherishing her children, her father, her mother, her cousins, weeping for the misfortunes of others, letting everything go in her household, and hating corsets;

—but so slow to move, so boring to listen to, with such a common appearance and such limited conversation, that he had never thought, even though she was thirty years old, that he was twenty, that they lived door to door, and that he spoke to her every day, that she could be a woman for someone, nor that she possessed anything of her sex other than the dress.
And then, what was there?
Binet, a few merchants, two or three innkeepers, the priest, and finally Mr.
Tuvache, the mayor, with his two sons, well-off people, gruff, obtuse, cultivating their own land, having family feasts, devout besides, and part of a completely unbearable society.
But against the common backdrop of all these human faces, Emma's figure stood out, isolated and yet more distant; for he felt between her and himself like vague abysses.
As soon as the first cold weather arrived, Emma left her room to inhabit the hall, a long room with a low ceiling where there was, on the mantelpiece, a dense polypore spreading against the mirror.
Sitting in her armchair, near the window, she saw the villagers passing by on the sidewalk.
Léon, twice a day, went from his study to the Lion d'Or.
Emma, from afar, heard him coming; she leaned in to listen, and the young man slipped behind the curtain, always dressed the same way and without turning his head.
But at dusk, when, with her chin in her left hand, she had abandoned her unfinished tapestry on her lap, she often started at the sudden appearance of that shadow gliding.
She would get up and order that the table be set.
